# README.md

# ai-ui-rewrite-rust

A Rust port of [assistant-ui](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui): chat runtime, AI SDK and assistant-stream
wire decoders, and a Slint thread UI, for native and WebAssembly apps.

- Runtime crates (`ai-ui-core`, `-stream`, `-data-stream`, `-http`, `-state`) have no UI dependency; the gate builds
  them for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- Follows upstream module for module at one pinned commit, so a backend that serves assistant-ui clients needs no change.
- Per-update cost does not grow with thread length: a bounded change journal projects only changed rows
  ([how](docs/guide/07-performance.md)).
- Markdown is formatted on a worker-thread pool, settled blocks once and the live tail on each delta.
- Native demo is one Rust binary with no JavaScript engine: `cargo run -p ai-ui-example-thread`.

Against upstream assistant-ui (`@assistant-ui/react` 0.15.33 in headless Chromium) on the same workload: a
1000-message thread, then a 9 KB prompt whose reply streams for 60 s. Rust is a release build that rasterises in
software. Four independent runs on 2026-11-11, each 5 to 9 interleaved pairs, under different power settings and load.
Each cell gives the range of the four run medians; the ratio's first number is the least favourable run
([RUNS](docs/RUNS.md); every raw file is in `benchmarks/results/`):

| | Rust | React | React / Rust |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open the thread, Markdown formatted and painted | 83-105 ms | 1385-2940 ms | 16.6x to 27.9x |
| Longest iteration or frame while streaming | 5.8-34 ms | 250-917 ms | 23.8x to 42.7x |
| Memory at the end (Rust RSS, React PSS) | 29.1-30.2 MiB | 850-1032 MiB | 28.2x to 35.4x |
| Process CPU while streaming 60 s | 4.3-17.2 s | 59.9-73.3 s | 4.2x to 14.0x |

Rust was ahead in every pair of every run. Absolute numbers depend on CPU speed and load: React's open time is the
more sensitive, so the open ratio is smallest on the fastest runs. Ratios are rounded down.

> Status: early. All ten library crates are on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/ai-ui-core) as 0.1; the two Slint
> crates need a one-line femtovg patch for now ([Using the crates](#using-the-crates)). Not yet ported:
> assistant-transport as a runtime, attachments, speech, custom per-tool components ([STATUS](docs/STATUS.md)). A port,
> not affiliated with the assistant-ui or Vercel AI SDK projects.

Try the WebAssembly demo with 10,000 messages on the [landing page](https://iyiolacak.github.io/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/).
Start with [Why ai-ui](docs/guide/00-why-ai-ui.md) or [Getting started](docs/guide/01-getting-started.md); every
number is in [RESULTS](docs/RESULTS.md); the browser build is described in [WEB](docs/WEB.md).

## Quickstart

### With a coding agent

Most people add this by asking their coding agent. Paste this into Claude Code (or any coding agent) in your project:

```text
Add ai-ui (a Rust port of assistant-ui: chat runtime, AI SDK streaming, Markdown, an optional Slint chat UI) to this project.

1. Get the skill: download https://iyiolacak.github.io/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/skill/ai-ui/SKILL.md and every reference file it links into .claude/skills/ai-ui/, keeping the same relative paths. If you can't write there, read them from those URLs instead.
2. Follow the skill. Inspect this project first, then tell me what you found and which crates you plan to add before changing anything.
3. Then do the work: add the crates, wire them up, and finish with cargo build, cargo clippy -- -D warnings, cargo test and one message actually sent and streamed back. Report what you changed, what you ran, and anything you couldn't verify.
```

To talk it through first, a "discuss first" prompt, the Claude Code skill (`skills/ai-ui/`) and `llms.txt` context for
any agent are on the [agents page](https://iyiolacak.github.io/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/agents/).

### By hand

```sh
cargo add ai-ui-core
```

```rust
use ai_ui_core::{adapter, AppendMessage, ChatModelRunResult, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime};

let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(
    |_options| adapter::from_results([Ok(ChatModelRunResult::text("Hello!"))]),
    LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
);
let run = runtime.append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Hi"))?;
// Drive `run` on any executor: slint::spawn_local, a Tokio LocalSet, wasm-bindgen-futures...
```

That snippet is built as [`crates/ai-ui-core/examples/quickstart.rs`](crates/ai-ui-core/examples/quickstart.rs).
For a full app, run the Slint example: `cargo run -p ai-ui-example-thread` (add `--api URL` for an AI SDK endpoint).

## Crates

| Crate | Upstream | Contents | wasm32 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ai-ui-core` | `@assistant-ui/core` | Message model (upstream JSON shape), branching `MessageRepository`, `ChatModelAdapter`, `ThreadRuntime` with local and external-store runtimes, `ThreadList`, tools and approvals, composers | yes |
| `ai-ui-stream` | `assistant-stream` | Stream chunks, message accumulator, state operations, incremental partial JSON, `assistant-transport` SSE | yes |
| `ai-ui-data-stream` | `@assistant-ui/react-data-stream` | `ChatModelAdapter` for AI SDK backends: request conversion, UI message stream and data stream responses | yes |
| `ai-ui-sdk-stream` | AI SDK `readUIMessageStream` | Exact AI SDK 7 UI-message-stream reducer, checked against the published package | yes |
| `ai-ui-http` | (fetch in upstream) | HTTP clients for the adapter: native (ureq + rustls) and browser `fetch` | yes |
| `ai-ui-state` | scoped state (`MessageState`...) | `ThreadView`: UI-agnostic state and actions over any runtime, smooth streaming clock | yes |
| `ai-ui-markdown` | `@assistant-ui/markdown` | Bounded Markdown parsing and the streaming block splitter | yes |
| `ai-ui-clipboard` | (browser clipboard) | Result-aware copy for native and browser | yes |
| `ai-ui-markdown-slint` | (react-markdown renderers) | Markdown to Slint rich text, off-thread formatting, streaming cache | via the example |
| `ai-ui-slint` | `@assistant-ui/react` UI | Slint thread, messages, composer and actions | via the example |
| `examples/thread` | assistant-ui default thread | Demo app: built-in streaming model or any AI SDK endpoint; native and browser | demo build |

All ten library crates are published on crates.io (the first eight have no UI dependency); the example is
`publish = false`. Portions are ported from assistant-ui (MIT, (c) AgentbaseAI Inc.); see [NOTICE](NOTICE).

## Performance

The latest measured Rust improvements and their reproduction commands are in
[`docs/PERFORMANCE.md`](docs/PERFORMANCE.md): incremental long-thread projection,
faster stream decoding, cooperative scheduling and bounded large-prompt layout.

Against upstream assistant-ui (React) on the same workload, measured with
[`benchmarks/react-baseline`](benchmarks/react-baseline) (whole-process CPU and
memory, same streamed reply, 60 s window; median of 5 interleaved pairs, release build, software renderer on the Rust side,
2026-11-11):

| | Rust | React |
|---|---|---|
| CPU while streaming into a 1000-message thread | 17.2 s | 73.3 s |
| Opening a 1000-message thread, until Markdown is formatted and shown | 0.11 s | 2.9 s |
| Memory with 1000 messages | 30 MiB | 1.4 GiB RSS, 0.8 GiB PSS (9 processes) |
| Longest stall while streaming a 40 KB prompt (200 messages) | 0.11 s | 2.4 s |

The open row compares like with like: Rust until the last message's Markdown is formatted and painted (105 ms; the rows
are visible after 13 ms, but that is not what React's 2.9 s measures), React until all messages and their Markdown are
rendered. Method, caveats and more numbers: [`docs/RESULTS.md`](docs/RESULTS.md) and [`docs/STATUS.md`](docs/STATUS.md#performance).

## Using the crates

`ai-ui-slint`, `ai-ui-markdown-slint` and the `examples/thread` app add a Slint UI. Until a Slint release uses
femtovg 0.28 (or femtovg publishes a 0.27.x with the fix), an app using Slint's FemtoVG-WGPU renderer should add this
to its `Cargo.toml`; without it a streaming chat uses about twice the CPU in a GPU window
([patches/README.md](patches/README.md)):

```toml
[patch.crates-io]
femtovg = { git = "https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust" }
```

**Slint licence.** This project's code is MIT. Slint itself is available under GPL-3.0, the Slint Royalty-Free
licence (requires an attribution badge) or a commercial licence; an application using the Slint crates must comply
with the one it chooses. See [THIRD_PARTY.md](THIRD_PARTY.md). Contributions: [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md);
security reports: [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md); changes: [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

# docs/guide/00-why-ai-ui.md

---
title: Why ai-ui
description: What ai-ui is, what it gives you that you can check, how it compares with upstream assistant-ui on the same workload, and where its limits are.
order: 0
section: Start
---

# Why ai-ui

**What this page gives you.** The case for ai-ui in one place: the problem it addresses, what you can verify about it,
a small like-for-like results table with its conditions, and the limits. Each claim points to a file or a command.

## The problem

A chat thread grows. A reply streams in as many small updates, a few bytes at a time. In a UI where each update
re-renders, re-lays out or re-parses work that scales with the whole thread, the cost of one update grows with the
number of messages, not with the size of the change.

In upstream assistant-ui on React, that looks like this on our benchmark: with 1000 messages the longest frame interval
while streaming was 916.6 ms (median of 5 interleaved pairs, range 866.6 to 1183.3 ms), and the main thread was busy for
about the whole 60 s window. With 10,000 messages, opening the thread took 26.1 s. Conditions and caveats are in the
table below and in [RESULTS](../RESULTS.md).

## What ai-ui is

ai-ui is a Rust port of [assistant-ui](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui), module for module at one pinned
upstream commit: the message model with branching, a chat runtime, tool calls with approvals, the AI SDK and
assistant-stream wire protocols, a UI-agnostic state layer, and a Slint thread UI with Markdown. The runtime crates
have no UI dependency, so a native app, a WebAssembly app or your own UI toolkit can use them. A backend that already
serves assistant-ui clients needs no change.

## What you get

- **Runtime crates with no UI dependency.** `ai-ui-core`, `ai-ui-stream`, `ai-ui-data-stream`, `ai-ui-http` and
  `ai-ui-state` do not depend on Slint or any windowing code. See the [crate reference](06-crates.md).
- **wasm32 is checked by the gate.** `scripts/gate.sh` runs `cargo build --locked --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` for
  the eight toolkit-independent crates (the full gate, not `--quick`). The Slint demo has its own web build; see
  [Running on the web](05-web.md).
- **Wire-compatible decoders.** The AI SDK UI message stream, the AI SDK data stream and assistant-transport are decoded
  incrementally, with reads that may split anywhere, including inside a UTF-8 character. 96 protocol vectors are saved in
  `crates/ai-ui-stream/tests/fixtures/protocol-vectors.json`; the counts are below.
- **Per-update cost that does not grow with thread length.** A bounded change journal in `ai-ui-core` lets a view
  project only the rows that changed. The mechanism is in [Performance](07-performance.md); the end-to-end measurements
  are in the table.
- **Markdown formatted off the UI thread.** `ai-ui-markdown` uses a pool of worker threads, formats settled blocks once
  and re-formats only the live tail while text streams (`crates/ai-ui-markdown/src/pool.rs`).
- **One native binary, no JavaScript engine.** `cargo run -p ai-ui-example-thread` builds and runs the demo; there is no
  Node or browser process in the native case.
- **Measured against upstream, with ranges.** Every figure comes from `docs/results.json`, is generated into
  [RESULTS](../RESULTS.md), and is checked by `python3 scripts/results.py check`.
- **Your own backend or none.** `LocalThreadRuntime` with a custom `ChatModelAdapter` needs no network; an
  [AI SDK endpoint](03-streaming-and-backends.md) is one flag in the example (`--api URL`).

## Measured against upstream assistant-ui

Rust is this repository's example app with the software renderer (`--bench-render`); React is upstream assistant-ui
(`@assistant-ui/react` 0.15.33) in headless Chromium. Same history, same demo reply, 60 s window. Medians of 5
interleaved pairs, measured 2026-11-11, machine load about 4-6. Ranges are min to max over the 5 runs. A second, independent run (9 pairs, lighter load) is in
[Performance](07-performance.md#second-run) and [RESULTS](../RESULTS.md). Across all four runs of that day the ratios were 16.6x to 27.9x for open, 23.8x to 42.7x for the longest stall, 28.2x to 35.4x for memory and 4.2x to 14.0x for CPU (medians per run; [RUNS](../RUNS.md)).

| Workload | Measure | Rust | React | Ratio (range) | RESULTS row |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1000 messages | open the thread, Markdown formatted and painted | 105.3 ms (100.8 to 150.9) | 2940 ms (2794 to 2987) | 27.9x (18.5x to 29.6x) | 15 |
| 1000 messages | longest iteration or frame while streaming | 34 ms (17.5 to 35.4) | 916.6 ms (866.6 to 1183.3) | 26.9x (24.4x to 67.6x) | 7 |
| 1000 messages | memory at the end, Rust RSS vs React PSS | 30.1 MiB (29.7 to 30.4) | 850.3 MiB (841.8 to 895.4) | 28.2x (27.6x to 30.1x) | 14 |
| 1000 messages | process CPU while streaming 60 s | 17160 ms (13700 to 17650) | 73260 ms (73050 to 73540) | 4.2x (4.1x to 5.3x) | 18 |
| 10,000 messages | open the thread, Markdown formatted and painted | 435.5 ms (382.9 to 472.1) | 26081 ms (23591 to 27196) | 59.8x (49.9x to 71x) | 6 |

Conditions that apply to every row:

- **Like for like.** "Open" is the same end state on both sides. Rust: until the last message's Markdown is formatted
  and painted at least once. React: until all messages are in the DOM with their Markdown rendered. Rust's first sync
  alone (12.9 ms at 1000 messages) is an earlier event and is not compared.
- **Memory.** PSS is the conservative figure for React because it discounts shared pages. React RSS summed over all
  Chromium processes was 1481.5 MiB for the same run (row 11).
- **Rust CPU includes software rasterisation.** React CPU is the whole Chromium process tree.
- **Ratios** are computed from the stated values and floored to one decimal. The range pairs the best Rust run with the
  worst React run and the reverse.
- **Not measured here:** a GPU window against React with a GPU, other browsers, other machines, and scenarios other than
  these two prompts. Stalls from single events are noisy; read the range, not just the median.

Method and reproduction commands: [Performance](07-performance.md). The earlier "24x" open figure, which compared
Rust before Markdown was formatted with React after, was withdrawn and is explained in RESULTS.

## How it works

A streamed update changes one message. The repository records which selected-path message changed in a bounded journal;
each `ThreadView` reads its own cursor and projects only those rows, falling back to a full projection when the thread's
shape changed or the cursor expired. The Slint host compares row identities (messages are `Arc`, so that is a pointer
comparison) and updates changed rows in place. The details, with file names, are in [Performance](07-performance.md).

Markdown is the other large cost. Parsing happens on worker threads, the newest source per key wins, and the UI keeps
showing formatted text while newer text is pending. Visible parts are submitted first. In the browser there are no
threads, so a wasm-only inline backend is used.

The design rules that make this possible (immutable `Arc` messages, a runtime free of I/O and clocks, adapters that yield
cumulative results) are described in [Concepts](02-concepts.md).

## Who it is for

- Rust apps, native or WebAssembly, that need a chat thread with branching, tools and approvals.
- Teams with a backend that already speaks the AI SDK protocols or assistant-transport.
- People who want the chat runtime without a UI toolkit and will write their own view on `ai-ui-state`.

## Who it is not for

- Projects that need features on the not-yet-ported list: assistant-transport as a runtime, a concrete HTTP remote
  thread-list adapter, LangGraph and other framework adapters, custom per-tool components, attachment, speech,
  dictation, suggestion and history adapters, message queue.
- Web apps that already run well on React and have no reason to change. The port does not remove the need for a Rust
  toolchain.

## Status and limits

- **Early.** All ten library crates are on crates.io as 0.1 (minor versions may break the API before 1.0). With Slint's
  FemtoVG-WGPU renderer, an app adds a one-line femtovg patch until a Slint release includes the fix
  (`patches/README.md`).
- **Browser demo.** It needs WebGL. On a 2x display the canvas renders at 1x and looks soft (known issue). Frame rates
  measured in headless Chromium use software WebGL and are a floor.
- **Fidelity.** Markdown styling in a real GPU window is marked unverified in [STATUS](../STATUS.md).
- **Protocol conformance.** As of 2026-11-09 ([PROTOCOL](../PROTOCOL.md#conformance-status)): 22 of 23 assistant-stream
  vectors that were run match (2 skipped), and 52 of 65 AI SDK vectors match, with each of the 13 differences recorded
  with its reason. The tests are the current truth.
- **Slint licence.** The code is MIT. Slint is GPL-3.0, a royalty-free licence with a badge, or commercial; apps that use
  the Slint crates must comply with the one they choose.
- **Independent project.** A port, not affiliated with the assistant-ui or Vercel AI SDK projects.

## Where to start

- [Getting started](01-getting-started.md): a first runtime in 20 lines, a first window, a first web build.
- [Concepts](02-concepts.md): the message model and runtimes.
- [Performance](07-performance.md): why the numbers look like this, and how to reproduce them.
- [Coming from assistant-ui](08-from-assistant-ui.md): parity table and differences.
- [RESULTS](../RESULTS.md) and [STATUS](../STATUS.md): the full tables and the ported and not-ported lists.

# docs/guide/01-getting-started.md

---
title: Getting started
description: Install ai-ui from git, run a first chat runtime in a few lines, stream a reply into the state layer and run the example app.
order: 1
section: Start
---

# Getting started

**What this page gives you.** This page takes you from an empty project to a running chat runtime: install from git, a first runtime in 20 lines, a streamed reply read through the state layer, the example app and a web build. Each snippet is built by the repository's tests or examples.

ai-ui is a Rust port of [assistant-ui](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui). It gives native and
WebAssembly Rust apps the same building blocks that assistant-ui gives React apps: a message model with branching,
a chat runtime that drives a model adapter, tool calls with approvals, the AI SDK and assistant-stream wire
protocols, and a Slint thread UI. It follows upstream's architecture module for module, so a backend that already
serves assistant-ui clients keeps working. The pinned upstream commit and the list of what is and is not ported are in
[STATUS](../STATUS.md).

It is early: the library crates are on crates.io as 0.1 (`cargo add ai-ui-core`). It is a port, not a product of the assistant-ui or Vercel AI SDK projects.

The point of the port is cost. On the same workload, a Rust thread uses much less CPU and memory than upstream's React
thread. One example, with its conditions: opening a 1000-message thread (9 KB prompt) until every message's Markdown is
formatted and painted took 105 ms for Rust and 2.94 s for React, median of 5 interleaved pairs, release build, software
renderer on the Rust side, headless Chromium for React, measured on 2026-11-11; across four runs that day the open ratio was 16.6x to 27.9x
([RUNS](../RUNS.md)). Other workloads, ranges and caveats are
in [RESULTS](../RESULTS.md); [Performance](07-performance.md) explains where the difference comes from.

## What you get

Three layers, each usable without the next:

| Layer | Crates | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Runtime | `ai-ui-core`, `ai-ui-stream`, `ai-ui-data-stream`, `ai-ui-http` | Messages, branches, the run loop, tools, wire decoders, HTTP clients. No UI dependency. |
| State | `ai-ui-state` | `ThreadView`: what a UI renders (rows, parts, branch numbers, smooth text) and the actions it calls. UI-agnostic. |
| UI | `ai-ui-slint`, `ai-ui-markdown-slint`, `examples/thread` | A Slint thread, composer and Markdown renderer, plus the demo app. |

The first two layers compile for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Every crate is described in the [crate reference](06-crates.md).

## Install

Using a coding agent? The [README](../../README.md#with-a-coding-agent) has a prompt to paste; it follows this guide.
By hand:

```toml
[dependencies]
ai-ui-core = "0.1"
ai-ui-state = "0.1"
# Only if you talk to an AI SDK backend:
ai-ui-data-stream = "0.1"
ai-ui-http = "0.1"
# The examples on this page drive futures with a small executor:
futures-executor = "0.3"
```

The non-UI crates need Rust 1.85 or newer
(`ai-ui-markdown` needs 1.88, the Slint crates 1.92). The runtime has no executor of its own, so you choose one:
`slint::spawn_local`, a Tokio `LocalSet`, `wasm-bindgen-futures`, or `futures_executor::block_on` in tests and scripts.

## A first runtime

A runtime holds one thread. Its model is a `ChatModelAdapter`: any closure from the run options to a stream of results
works. This one answers every request with a canned text.

```rust
use ai_ui_core::{
    adapter, AppendMessage, ChatModelRunResult, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime,
};

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // The adapter is the model. This one answers every step with a canned text.
    let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(
        |_options| adapter::from_results([Ok(ChatModelRunResult::text("Hello!"))]),
        LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
    );

    // `append` changes the thread now: the user message and an empty, running
    // assistant message exist before the run has been polled.
    let run = runtime.append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Hi"))?;
    println!("before the run: {} messages", runtime.messages().len());

    // The returned future does the model work. Any executor can drive it.
    futures_executor::block_on(run)?;

    for message in runtime.messages().iter() {
        println!("{:?}: {}", message.role(), message.text());
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

Running it prints:

```text
before the run: 2 messages
User: Hi
Assistant: Hello!
```

Two things to notice. First, `append` does its synchronous work immediately: the user message and a running, still
empty assistant message are in the thread before anything is awaited, which is what lets a UI show them in the same
frame. Second, the future it returns is the model run. Nothing happens until you spawn it. The same code is built as
[`quickstart.rs`](https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/blob/main/crates/ai-ui-core/examples/quickstart.rs):
`cargo run --example quickstart -p ai-ui-core`.

## Stream a reply and read the state

A real model streams. Each item an adapter yields is the whole reply so far, not a delta (the
[concepts page](02-concepts.md#chatmodeladapter-and-run-results) explains why). A UI does not read the runtime directly:
it holds a `ThreadView` from `ai-ui-state`, reads `view.state()` when told something changed, and calls the view's
actions (`send`, `stop`, `reload`, `switch_branch`, ...).

```rust
use ai_ui_core::{
    adapter, AssistantMessagePart, ChatModelRunResult, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime,
    PartStatus, RunError, TextPart,
};
use ai_ui_state::{PartKind, ThreadView, ViewOptions};
use std::cell::Cell;
use std::rc::Rc;

/// One cumulative update: the whole reply so far, and whether the part is still running.
fn step(text: &str, status: PartStatus) -> Result<ChatModelRunResult, RunError> {
    Ok(ChatModelRunResult::content(vec![
        AssistantMessagePart::Text(TextPart {
            status: Some(status),
            ..TextPart::new(text)
        }),
    ]))
}

fn reply(view: &ThreadView) -> String {
    match &view.state().messages[1].parts[0].kind {
        PartKind::Text { text, .. } => format!("{text:?}"),
        _ => String::new(),
    }
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(
        |_options| {
            adapter::from_results([
                step("Rust", PartStatus::Running),
                step("Rust is a", PartStatus::Running),
                step("Rust is a systems language.", PartStatus::Complete),
            ])
        },
        LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
    );
    let view = ThreadView::new(Rc::new(runtime), ViewOptions::default());

    // A UI reads `state()` whenever it is told something changed. That is also
    // how the view notices a part that is still streaming and starts to pace it.
    let changes = Rc::new(Cell::new(0u32));
    let _subscription = view.subscribe({
        let (view, changes) = (view.clone(), changes.clone());
        move || {
            changes.set(changes.get() + 1);
            let _ = view.state();
        }
    });

    let run = view
        .send("What is Rust?")?
        .expect("the composer was not empty");
    futures_executor::block_on(run)?;
    println!("run finished, shown so far: {}", reply(&view));

    // Once per frame the UI hands the view a clock reading.
    let mut now_ms = 0.0;
    while view.needs_frame() {
        now_ms += 16.0;
        view.tick(now_ms);
        if now_ms == 64.0 {
            println!("after 64 ms: {}", reply(&view));
        }
    }
    println!("after {now_ms} ms: {}", reply(&view));
    println!(
        "running: {}, notifications: {}",
        view.state().is_running,
        changes.get()
    );
    Ok(())
}
```

Its output:

```text
run finished, shown so far: ""
after 64 ms: "Rust is a"
after 160 ms: "Rust is a systems language."
running: false, notifications: 16
```

The model finished at once, but the view reveals the text at a steady pace, like upstream's `useSmooth`. A frame loop
calls `view.tick(now_ms)` while `view.needs_frame()` is true; here the loop is simulated with a 16 ms step. The notification
count varies with the library version and is only printed to show that the subscription fired. In a real app the
callback asks the UI toolkit for a redraw instead of reading state itself.

The text part is marked `PartStatus::Running` in the first two results. That is how the view knows a part is streaming
and paces it. The wire decoders set it for you; a hand-written adapter has to set it to get smooth text.

## Run the example app

`examples/thread` is assistant-ui's default thread in Slint: sidebar with threads, messages, reasoning and tool
disclosure, branch picker, copy, edit and regenerate, a composer and a settings panel. It needs the system fontconfig
development package (see [troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)) and Rust 1.92.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust
cd ai-ui-rewrite-rust
cargo run -p ai-ui-example-thread --release
```

With no flags it runs a built-in demo model that streams reasoning and then a Markdown answer. A prompt that contains
"weather" makes it call the `get_weather` tool, which runs without asking. A prompt that contains "email" calls
`send_email`, which stops and asks you to approve first. Flags go after `--` when you use `cargo run`; they are the
real ones from `examples/thread/src/main.rs`:

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--api URL` | Talk to an AI SDK endpoint instead of the demo model (native build only). |
| `--header NAME:VALUE` | Add a request header with `--api`, for example an authorization header. |
| `--theme system\|light\|dark`, `--light` | Choose the theme for this run. |
| `--text-scale F` | Text size factor, clamped to 0.75 to 2.0. |
| `--reading-width compact\|default\|wide\|xwide\|full` | Width of the message column. |
| `--open-settings` | Start with the settings panel open. |
| `--history N` | Start with N messages already in the thread. |
| `--long-reply-kb K` | Ask the demo model for a reply of about K kilobytes of Markdown. |
| `--token-delay-ms MS` | Pause between demo tokens (default 18). |
| `--ask TEXT` | Run a prompt immediately; repeatable. |
| `--decide allow\|deny` | Answer a pending approval automatically. |
| `--new-thread` | Open a new thread first. |
| `--size WxH` | Window or screenshot size (default 900x760). |

Settings changed in the sidebar are saved in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/ai-ui-example-thread/settings.json`; flags override them
for one run. A scenario that exercises the long-thread paths:

```sh
cargo run -p ai-ui-example-thread --release -- --history 1000 --long-reply-kb 9 --token-delay-ms 4
```

To try the approval flow without clicking: `-- --ask "Send an email to the team" --decide allow`.

For a GPU renderer, build with `--features gpu-window` and set `SLINT_BACKEND=winit-femtovg`. The default build includes
Slint's software renderer, which also powers the headless flags: `--screenshot out.png` renders offscreen and exits (with
`--conversation`, `--expand-all`, `--mid-stream MS`). The software renderer draws styled text as plain characters, so
screenshots do not show bold or list styling; see the visual fidelity note in [STATUS](../STATUS.md#visual-fidelity).
`--bench N` and its relatives are the benchmark harness, covered in [Performance](07-performance.md).

To point it at your own backend: `cargo run -p ai-ui-example-thread --release -- --api http://localhost:3000/api/chat`.
What that request and response look like is in [Streaming and backends](03-streaming-and-backends.md).

## In the browser

The same example builds for WebAssembly and runs the demo model in a canvas. `scripts/build-web-demo.sh` produces the
JavaScript glue and the `.wasm` file. Flags become query parameters there (`?history=1000&light`). The build steps, what
works in the browser and its limits are in [Running on the web](05-web.md) and [WEB](../WEB.md).

## Troubleshooting

**`fontconfig` not found when building a Slint crate.** The Slint crates link the system fontconfig. Install the
development package: `libfontconfig1-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu, `fontconfig-devel` on Fedora. If it lives in a
non-standard prefix, point pkg-config at it before building:

```sh
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH=/path/to/prefix/lib/pkgconfig
```

The runtime and state crates do not need fontconfig, so `ai-ui-core`, `ai-ui-state`, `ai-ui-stream`, `ai-ui-data-stream`
and `ai-ui-http` build without it.

**`wasm-bindgen` version mismatch.** `scripts/build-web-demo.sh` stops with "wasm-bindgen is X but Cargo.lock needs Y"
when the command-line tool differs from the library locked in `Cargo.lock` (0.2.129 at the time of writing). Install that
exact version of the CLI, or set `WASM_BINDGEN=/path/to/wasm-bindgen`. Add the target once with
`rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown`.

**Old toolchain.** The Slint crates and the example need Rust 1.92; `rustup update` fixes most "requires rustc" errors.

**Your own Slint app drops frames during long streams.** Slint 1.18 depends on a femtovg release that recompiles GPU
pipelines too often for a streaming chat. This workspace carries a patch; an app that uses the Slint crates adds:

```toml
[patch.crates-io]
femtovg = { git = "https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust" }
```

 See [patches/README.md](https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/blob/main/patches/README.md).

**Slint licence.** The code here is MIT, but Slint is available under GPL-3.0, a royalty-free licence that requires an
attribution badge, or a commercial licence. An app using the Slint crates must comply with the one it picks.

- [Concepts](02-concepts.md): the message model, branches, runtimes, tools, smooth streaming and the state layer.
- [Streaming and backends](03-streaming-and-backends.md): wire protocols and connecting a real backend.
- [Building a UI with Slint](04-ui-slint.md): the thread UI in detail.

# docs/guide/02-concepts.md

---
title: Concepts
description: The message model, branching repository, runtimes, thread list, adapters, tools and approvals, smooth streaming and the state layer, and why each exists.
order: 2
section: Start
