# Concepts

**What this page gives you.** This page defines the types you will use: messages and parts, the branching repository, `ThreadRuntime`, adapters, tools and approvals, smooth streaming and `ThreadView`. For each it says where the code lives and why it has that shape.

This page walks through the ideas the rest of the guide builds on, in the order data moves: a message, the tree of
messages, the runtime that owns the tree, the adapter that produces model output, tools, smooth streaming, and finally
the state layer a UI reads. Each section says what the thing is, where it lives, and why it is shaped that way. Two goals
explain most of the shapes:

- **Correctness against upstream.** Types and behaviours follow [assistant-ui](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui)
  at one pinned commit, and tests are ported from upstream's, so a thread, a backend or a stored history means the same
  thing in both worlds.
- **Cost per streamed update.** A chat spends most of its life receiving one small update after another. The design keeps
  the work for one update independent of how long the thread is, wherever it can.

## The message model

Types live in [`crates/ai-ui-core/src/types.rs`](https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/blob/main/crates/ai-ui-core/src/types.rs).
A `ThreadMessage` is one of three roles (`MessageRole`): `System`, `User` or `Assistant`.

| Role | Struct | Content parts (`type` tag) |
|---|---|---|
| System | `SystemMessage` | `text` |
| User | `UserMessage` | `text`, `image`, `file`, `data`, `audio`, plus `attachments` |
| Assistant | `AssistantMessage` | `text`, `reasoning`, `tool-call`, `source`, `file`, `image`, `data`, `generative-ui` |

Only assistant messages have a `status` (`MessageStatus`), because only they are produced over time:

- `Running`: the run is in progress.
- `RequiresAction { reason }`: paused until the app or the user acts, for tool calls or an interrupt.
- `Complete { reason }`: finished, with `Stop` or `Unknown`.
- `Incomplete { reason, error }`: ended early, because it was cancelled, hit a length or content filter, reached the step
  limit with tool calls pending, or failed (`Error`, with the error detail stored on the message).

Parts have their own `PartStatus` (`Running`, `Complete`, `Incomplete`). That is how a UI knows which paragraph is still
growing. A tool call is a part (`ToolCallPart`) that carries its arguments (`args` parsed, `args_text` raw), its `result`,
`is_error`, an optional `approval` and an optional `interrupt`, so a call and its answer live in one place.

Two design choices matter here.

**The JSON shape is upstream's.** Tags are `type` and `role`, field names are camelCase, `createdAt` is epoch
milliseconds, and fields this port does not model are kept in an `extra` map and written back out. A message exported
from one side imports on the other, and a backend that expects assistant-ui's message JSON does not need to know which
client sent it.

**Messages are shared, not copied.** The thread hands out `Arc<ThreadMessage>`. A streamed update replaces one `Arc`;
every other message keeps its pointer, which is what the state layer later uses to skip unchanged rows.

## The branching repository

`MessageRepository` ([`repository.rs`](https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/blob/main/crates/ai-ui-core/src/repository.rs))
stores a conversation as a tree, because a conversation with edit and regenerate is not a list. Each message has one
`parent_id` (`None` for a root). Messages that share a parent are *siblings*, and each parent remembers which child is
selected. The *head* is the last message of the *selected path* that runs from the root through the selected children.
`messages()` returns that path, and it is what the UI shows and what is sent to the model.

Branches are created by two operations, and both are ordinary appends under an existing parent:

- **Regenerate** answers the same user message again. Call `start_run` with `parent_id` set to the user message and
  `source_id` set to the answer being replaced. The new answer becomes a sibling of the old one and is selected.
- **Edit** replaces a user message. Append a user message with the edited message's parent and `source_id` set to the
  edited message. The edited text becomes a sibling of the original, and its answer follows it. A `Composer` from
  `begin_edit` does this for you when you `send` it.

`switch_to_branch(id)` selects the branch containing `id`, and `branches(id)` lists a message and its siblings.
`branch_position(id)` gives the 1-based position and count that a "2 / 3" branch picker shows.

```rust
use ai_ui_core::{
    adapter, AppendMessage, ChatModelRunResult, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime,
    StartRunConfig, ThreadRuntime,
};
use std::cell::Cell;
use std::rc::Rc;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let calls = Rc::new(Cell::new(0));
    let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(
        {
            let calls = calls.clone();
            move |_options| {
                calls.set(calls.get() + 1);
                adapter::from_results([Ok(ChatModelRunResult::text(format!(
                    "answer {}",
                    calls.get()
                )))])
            }
        },
        LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
    );
    futures_executor::block_on(runtime.append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Hi"))?)?;
    let user = runtime.messages()[0].id().clone();
    let first = runtime.messages()[1].id().clone();

    // Regenerate: answer the same user message again, replacing `first` on the selected path.
    futures_executor::block_on(runtime.start_run(StartRunConfig {
        parent_id: Some(user.clone()),
        source_id: Some(first.clone()),
        ..Default::default()
    })?)?;
    println!("selected: {}", runtime.messages()[1].text());
    println!("siblings: {}", runtime.branches(&first)?.len());

    // Edit: append a user message with the same parent and a source_id.
    let mut edit = AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Hello");
    edit.source_id = Some(user.clone());
    futures_executor::block_on(runtime.append(edit)?)?;
    println!(
        "after edit: {:?}",
        runtime
            .messages()
            .iter()
            .map(|m| m.text())
            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
    );

    // Go back to the first answer's branch.
    runtime.switch_to_branch(&first)?;
    println!(
        "after switch: {:?}",
        runtime
            .messages()
            .iter()
            .map(|m| m.text())
            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
    );

    // Persist and restore.
    let saved = ThreadRuntime::export(&runtime);
    println!("exported {} messages", saved.messages.len());
    Ok(())
}
```

This prints:

```text
selected: answer 2
siblings: 2
after edit: ["Hello", "answer 3"]
after switch: ["Hi", "answer 1"]
exported 5 messages
```

The edit left the first branch intact: switching back to the original answer restores the original question too.
`export()` returns an `ExportedRepository` (every message with its parent, plus the head) and `import()` loads one, so a
history with all its branches survives a restart. Messages serialize with serde, so storage is up to you.
`ExportedRepository::from_linear` builds one from a plain list.

Errors that would corrupt the tree (a missing parent, a cycle) are `RepositoryError` values and leave the tree unchanged.
Upstream throws for these.

*Why a tree.* Edit and regenerate must never destroy what was there, and the model must only see the selected path. A
tree gives both for free. *Why this implementation.* Appending under the head is constant time, the selected path is cached
as one shared slice and patched in place when a streamed message replaces the head, and a bounded change journal records
which path indices changed (`message_changes_since`) plus a `shape_version` that only moves when messages are added,
moved or removed or the selection changes. Those two counters are what let a view of a long thread skip the messages that
did not change; see [the state layer](#the-state-layer) below.

## The ThreadRuntime trait

A UI never talks to a concrete runtime. It talks to the `ThreadRuntime` trait
([`runtime.rs`](https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/blob/main/crates/ai-ui-core/src/runtime.rs)):
`messages`, `is_running`, `capabilities`, `branches`, `switch_to_branch`, `append`, `reload`, `cancel_run`,
`add_tool_result`, `respond_to_tool_approval`, `submit_feedback`, composers, `subscribe_dyn`, `export` and `import`, plus
the two change counters from the previous section. `RuntimeCapabilities` says which of these the thread supports, so a
UI hides the edit button when `edit` is false instead of showing a button that fails.

Methods do their synchronous work at once and return a `RunFuture` for anything that must wait. They never spawn:
spawning belongs to your executor. The runtime is single-threaded (`Rc`) like upstream's UI-thread runtime, while
messages are `Arc` so an adapter can move them to a worker thread. Timestamps and ids come from `LocalRuntimeOptions`
(`clock`, `ids`), because `SystemTime` does not exist on `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.

There are three implementations, and one trait means the same UI works with all of them.

**`LocalThreadRuntime`**: the library drives the model. You give it a `ChatModelAdapter`, and it owns the run loop, the
repository, tools and composers. The examples in this guide use it.

**`ExternalStoreRuntime`**: your app owns the messages, the model call and the persistence, and the runtime displays them.
It is the Rust counterpart of upstream's `useExternalStoreRuntime`. You implement `ExternalStore` (`on_new`, and
optionally `on_edit`, `on_reload`, `on_cancel`, `on_add_tool_result`, `on_respond_to_tool_approval`, `on_feedback`,
`on_branch_change`), declare `capabilities`, and push state in with `set_messages`, `set_repository` and `set_running`.
Nothing is inserted optimistically. Messages you re-send unchanged keep their `Arc`, so an app that stores its own
messages does not make the view re-render the whole thread.

```rust
use ai_ui_core::{
    AppendMessage, ExternalStore, ExternalStoreRuntime, RuntimeCapabilities, StoreFuture,
    ThreadMessage, ThreadRuntime,
};
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

/// The app owns the messages; the runtime only shows them and forwards actions.
struct App {
    sent: Rc<RefCell<Vec<String>>>,
}

impl ExternalStore for App {
    fn on_new(&self, message: AppendMessage) -> StoreFuture {
        // Send it to your own backend here, then call `set_messages` with the new state.
        if let ai_ui_core::AppendContent::User { content, .. } = &message.content {
            self.sent
                .borrow_mut()
                .push(format!("{} part(s)", content.len()));
        }
        Box::pin(async { Ok(()) })
    }
    fn capabilities(&self) -> RuntimeCapabilities {
        RuntimeCapabilities {
            switch_to_branch: true,
            copy: true,
            cancel: true,
            edit: false,
            reload: false,
            feedback: false,
            answer_tool_call: false,
        }
    }
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let sent = Rc::new(RefCell::new(Vec::new()));
    let runtime = ExternalStoreRuntime::new(App { sent: sent.clone() });
    let hello: ThreadMessage = serde_json::from_value(serde_json::json!({
        "role": "user", "id": "m1", "createdAt": 0,
        "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "Hello" }]
    }))?;
    runtime.set_messages([hello]);
    futures_executor::block_on(runtime.append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "More"))?)?;
    println!(
        "{} message(s) shown, {:?} sent",
        runtime.messages().len(),
        sent.borrow()
    );
    Ok(())
}
```

**`ThreadList`**: many threads, one of them the main thread. Its factory creates one runtime per thread, so a list can mix
local and external-store threads. Switching, creating, renaming, archiving and deleting apply immediately and are
persisted by background tasks through an optional `ThreadListAdapter` (`list`, `initialize`, `rename`, `archive`,
`unarchive`, `delete`, `generate_title`, `load`); a failed task undoes its change and the message is available from
`last_error`. A new thread becomes a regular one when its first message appears. The host supplies a `Spawner` for the
background tasks. `ThreadView::for_list` follows the main thread and rebinds when it changes.

```rust
use ai_ui_core::{
    adapter, AppendMessage, ChatModelRunResult, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime, Spawner,
    ThreadList, ThreadRuntime,
};
use std::rc::Rc;

fn main() {
    // The factory builds one runtime per thread. Background work (persistence,
    // titles) goes to the host's executor; this one just drives it to completion.
    let spawner: Spawner = Rc::new(|future| futures_executor::block_on(future));
    let list = ThreadList::new(
        |_id| {
            Rc::new(LocalThreadRuntime::new(
                |_options| adapter::from_results([Ok(ChatModelRunResult::text("ok"))]),
                LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
            )) as Rc<dyn ThreadRuntime>
        },
        spawner,
        None,
    );
    let first = list.main_id();
    // A thread becomes a regular one when its first message appears.
    let run = list
        .main()
        .append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Hi"))
        .unwrap();
    futures_executor::block_on(run).unwrap();
    list.switch_to_new();
    println!(
        "regular: {}, main changed: {}",
        list.regular().len(),
        list.main_id() != first
    );
}
```

## ChatModelAdapter and run results

An adapter is the model: `fn run(&self, options: ChatModelRunOptions) -> RunStream`, where a `RunStream` is a stream of
`Result<ChatModelRunResult, RunError>`. Any closure with that signature is an adapter, and `adapter::once` and
`adapter::from_results` build streams for tests.

`ChatModelRunOptions` carries the selected path up to the message being answered, the `ModelContext` (system prompt,
tool definitions, call settings, config), an `AbortSignal`, the id of the assistant message being filled, the thread's
remote id, the parent id, and the assistant message as it stood when the step began, whose content is non-empty when a
run continues after tool results.

**Each result is cumulative.** A `ChatModelRunResult` holds the whole content so far, not a delta; the runtime replaces the
message content with it. This matches upstream, and it has three benefits. A consumer that falls behind simply sees a later,
fuller snapshot. There is no delta bookkeeping in the UI. And a decoder can fold every network read that is already
available into one result: `ai-ui-stream` does this so that `result()` runs once per wake-up, not once per slice of bytes.

A run ends in one of three ways:

- The stream ends: the message completes, or `RequiresAction` if the last step left unanswered tool calls.
- `RunError::Aborted` or `cancel_run`: the message becomes `incomplete/cancelled`, with the text received so far kept.
- `RunError::Failed { message, error }`: the message becomes `incomplete/error` with the detail stored on it, and the run
  future returns the error. Content received before the failure stays.

If the host drops the run future, the message is marked cancelled and the runtime stops running. The `AbortSignal`
(`AbortController` on the owner side) is thread-safe and can be polled or awaited, since adapters often do their I/O on
another thread. The runtime also stops polling an adapter that ignores the signal.

## Tools and approvals

A model can call tools. The tool definitions go to the model through `ModelContext`; the calls come back as `tool-call`
parts. A `Tool` with an `execute` function runs inside your app, after the model step that asked for it, and its result
feeds the next step. Tools are registered with `set_tools(ToolRegistry)`.

```rust
use ai_ui_core::adapter::{self, RunStream};
use ai_ui_core::{
    AppendMessage, AssistantMessagePart, ChatModelRunOptions, ChatModelRunResult,
    LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime, MessageStatus, RequiresActionReason, Tool,
    ToolCallPart, ToolRegistry,
};
use serde_json::json;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // Step 1 asks for the tool; step 2 sees its result and answers.
    let model = |options: ChatModelRunOptions| -> RunStream {
        match options
            .message
            .tool_calls()
            .next()
            .and_then(|c| c.result.clone())
        {
            None => adapter::from_results([Ok(ChatModelRunResult::content(vec![
                AssistantMessagePart::ToolCall(ToolCallPart {
                    tool_call_id: "call-1".into(),
                    tool_name: "get_weather".into(),
                    args: serde_json::from_value(json!({ "city": "Oslo" })).unwrap(),
                    args_text: r#"{"city":"Oslo"}"#.into(),
                    ..Default::default()
                }),
            ])
            .with_status(MessageStatus::RequiresAction {
                reason: RequiresActionReason::ToolCalls,
            }))]),
            Some(result) => adapter::from_results([Ok(ChatModelRunResult::text(format!(
                "It is {} degrees in Oslo.",
                result["temp_c"]
            )))]),
        }
    };
    let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(model, LocalRuntimeOptions::default());
    runtime.set_tools(
        ToolRegistry::new().with(
            "get_weather",
            Tool::new(json!({
                "type": "object",
                "properties": { "city": { "type": "string" } },
                "required": ["city"]
            }))
            .description("Current weather for a city")
            .execute(|_args, _context| async { Ok(json!({ "temp_c": 7 })) }),
        ),
    );
    futures_executor::block_on(
        runtime.append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Weather in Oslo?"))?,
    )?;
    println!("{}", runtime.messages().last().unwrap().text());
    Ok(())
}
```

That prints `It is 7 degrees in Oslo.` The run took two model steps: the first ended in `RequiresAction` with an open call,
the runtime ran `get_weather`, and the second step saw the result in `options.message`.

The controls around that loop:

- **`requires_approval()`** on a `Tool` makes the run pause before executing. The call gets a pending `ToolApproval` with a
  prompt (`approval_prompt(|name, args| ...)` customises the question), the run future resolves, and `is_running` is false.
  `respond_to_tool_approval(message_id, approval_id, approved, reason)` records the decision and returns a new `RunFuture`
  that resumes the run. Approving runs the tool. Denying never runs it; the model hears `{"error": reason}` as the tool
  result. A decided approval cannot be answered twice (`RuntimeError::ApprovalNotFound`).
- **`max_steps`** in `LocalRuntimeOptions` (default 2) limits model steps per run, so a model that keeps calling tools
  cannot loop forever. At the limit the message ends `incomplete/tool-calls`.
- **Human tools.** A call to a tool without `execute` is left for the host. Answer it with `add_tool_result`, which
  resumes the run when it answers the last open call. `human_tool_names` narrows which tools the run waits for.
- **Cancelling** aborts a running tool through the `AbortSignal` in its `ToolContext`.
- **Cut-off arguments never run.** If a response ends inside a tool call's argument JSON, the runtime gives the call an
  error result and neither executes it nor offers it for approval, whichever decoder produced it. A repaired partial value
  is a preview for display, not an instruction to act on.

Tools run one after another. Per-tool presentation goes through `ThreadView::set_tool_presenter`; a fully custom component
per tool (generative UI) is not ported. See [STATUS](../STATUS.md).

*Why this design.* Running tools in the runtime, not the UI, keeps the approval flow identical for every front end and
makes the dangerous cases (denied, cancelled, truncated) testable without a window.

## Smooth streaming

Model output arrives in bursts: a hundred characters, a pause, then three. Shown as received, that looks jerky.
`SmoothText` ([`smooth.rs`](https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/blob/main/crates/ai-ui-core/src/smooth.rs)) is a
port of upstream's `useSmooth`. It reveals a target text at a steady pace. Each character takes
`min(max_char_interval_ms, drain_ms / remaining)`, so a large backlog is revealed faster (it drains in about `drain_ms`),
while the last characters and a slow trickle are at most `max_char_interval_ms` apart. Defaults are 250 and 5 ms.
`max_chars_per_frame` caps the work per frame.

It is a plain state machine with no clock of its own: the caller passes `now_ms` to `tick`. That keeps it testable and
usable on `wasm32`, and it means the pacing follows the display's frame loop rather than a timer. If a regeneration
replaces the text with something that does not extend what is shown, it starts over. Revealing never splits a UTF-8
character. You normally do not use it directly: `ThreadView` creates one per streaming part (configured with
`ViewOptions { smooth }`) and exposes the pace through `tick` and `needs_frame`.

## The state layer

`ai-ui-state` is the boundary between runtimes and UIs. `ThreadView::new(runtime, options)` wraps any `ThreadRuntime`.
`view.state()` returns an `Arc<ThreadState>`:

- `ThreadState`: `messages: Vec<Arc<MessageState>>`, `is_empty`, `is_running`, `capabilities`.
- `MessageState`: `id`, `role`, `index`, `is_last`, `branch_number` and `branch_count`, `parts: Vec<PartState>`, the joined
  `text`, `status`, a readable `error`, `is_generating`, `is_copied`, `can_edit`, `can_reload`, `can_copy`,
  `can_feedback`, `feedback`, and the underlying message.
- `PartKind`: `Text`, `Reasoning`, `ToolCall` (with `ToolCallState`: arguments, result, `ToolStatus`, approval, expanded,
  `ToolPresentation`), `Source`, `Image`, `File`, `Data`, `GenerativeUi`.

The view also holds UI-local state that must not live in the runtime: smooth-text animators, which reasoning and tool
sections are expanded, and the "copied" confirmation. Actions mirror upstream's scoped actions: `send`, `stop`, `reload`,
`switch_branch`, `begin_edit`, `copy_text`, `toggle_part`, `respond_to_approval`, `add_tool_result`, `submit_feedback`.

*Why a state layer.* Upstream splits runtime, scoped state and primitives so that rendering logic does not depend on a
framework. Here that split has a second purpose: toolkit code reads one value and never touches the runtime, so a Slint
UI, a terminal UI or a test can sit on the same `ThreadView`.

*How it stays cheap.* The state is a vector of `Arc<MessageState>` rows, and a row that did not change is the same `Arc`
as before, so a UI finds what changed by pointer comparison. To rebuild rows, the view asks the runtime
`message_changes_since(its own cursor)`, which names the selected indices that changed since the view last looked. It
rebuilds those rows and keeps the others, and when the previous `ThreadState` is not held elsewhere it updates it in place.
`structure_version` tells it that no branch moved, so it reuses each row's branch position instead of looking it up. If the
runtime does not track changes, the journal no longer covers the view's cursor (it is bounded), or something global
changed (the thread started running, capabilities changed), the view falls back to a full pass. The fallback is the safe
path; the journal is an optimisation that must be correct whenever it is used. The `ai-ui-state` perf test and
[Performance](07-performance.md) show how this is measured.

## Data flow

The path from a backend to pixels, with the crate that owns each step:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B[(Model backend)] -->|HTTP body bytes| H["ai-ui-http: NativeClient / FetchClient"]
    subgraph adapter ["DataStreamAdapter (ai-ui-data-stream), a ChatModelAdapter"]
        H -->|ByteStream| D["Decoder (ai-ui-stream): SSE / data stream to Chunks"]
        D -->|Chunk| A[MessageAccumulator]
    end
    A -->|"cumulative ChatModelRunResult"| R["LocalThreadRuntime run loop (ai-ui-core)"]
    R -->|"add_or_update(Arc message)"| P[(MessageRepository + change journal)]
    R <-->|execute / approvals| T[ToolRegistry]
    P -->|notify| V["ThreadView (ai-ui-state)"]
    C["frame clock: tick(now_ms)"] --> V
    V -->|"Arc ThreadState, changed rows only"| U["UI (ai-ui-slint or your own)"]
    U -->|"send / stop / reload / switch_branch / approve"| V
    V -->|actions| R
```

Reading it left to right: bytes are decoded into chunks, the accumulator folds chunks into one cumulative message, and
the run loop stores it in the repository by replacing one `Arc`. The repository notifies subscribers, and the view turns
the change into new rows for exactly the messages that changed. The UI redraws those rows. Actions travel back the same
way. For an external-store thread, replace the left half with your own code calling `set_messages`; for a custom model,
replace the adapter box.

Next: [Streaming and backends](03-streaming-and-backends.md) covers the left half of the diagram. The architecture
decisions behind it are in [ARCHITECTURE](../ARCHITECTURE.md), and every crate is listed in the [crate reference](06-crates.md).

---

# docs/guide/03-streaming-and-backends.md

---
title: Streaming and backends
description: How model output becomes messages - chunks, decoders for the three wire protocols, the HTTP clients - and how to connect and test a real backend.
order: 3
section: Build
---

# Streaming and backends

**What this page gives you.** This page shows how bytes from a backend become messages: the four-stage pipeline, the three wire formats and their decoders, request building, the HTTP clients, a connection to a real backend, and how to test without a network.

[Concepts](02-concepts.md) described the runtime from the adapter inwards. This page covers the other side: how bytes from
a backend become the cumulative results an adapter yields, which wire formats are understood, how a request is built,
and how to connect and test a real backend. Byte-level detail lives in the reference documents
[PROTOCOL](../PROTOCOL.md) (the protocol audit and conformance record) and [AI-SDK-STREAM](../AI-SDK-STREAM.md) (the strict AI SDK 7
reducer); this page links to them rather than repeating them.

## The pipeline

Every network adapter does the same four things, and each has one type:

1. **Transport** (`HttpClient`, `ai-ui-data-stream`): send a request, return a status, headers and a `ByteStream` of body
   reads. The reads can split anywhere, including inside a UTF-8 character.
2. **Decoder** (`StreamDecoder`, `ai-ui-stream`): `push(bytes)` returns the `Chunk`s that are now complete, `finish()`
   flushes at end of input. Each wire format has one decoder.
3. **Accumulator** (`MessageAccumulator`): folds chunks into the assistant message and produces a `ChatModelRunResult`.
4. **Run stream** (`run_stream`): ties the three together and yields the cumulative result to the runtime.

### Chunks

A `Chunk` is the one internal vocabulary all wire formats are translated into, modelled on assistant-stream's
`AssistantStreamChunk`. A chunk has a `path` (the index of the part it applies to) and a `ChunkKind`: `PartStart` (a
`PartInit` of text, reasoning, tool call, source, file or data), `PartFinish`, `TextDelta`, `ToolCallArgsTextFinish`,
`ToolCallApproval`, `Annotations`, `Data`, `StepStart`, `StepFinish`, `MessageFinish`, `Result` (a tool result), `Error` and
`UpdateState`. Tool arguments arrive as `TextDelta`s on a tool-call part. One vocabulary means a new wire format needs only a
decoder, and everything after it (the accumulator, the runtime, tool continuation, the UI) is shared.

### The accumulator

`MessageAccumulator` applies chunks in order and never panics on bad input: an invalid chunk is dropped and recorded in
`warnings()`. `result()` builds the cumulative `ChatModelRunResult`, `status()` reports `Running` until the message
finishes, and `finish()` settles a message at a clean end of stream: `RequiresAction` if a tool call is still open,
otherwise `Complete`. Configurable `Limits` bound tool-argument size and state size so a hostile or broken stream cannot
allocate without limit.

`run_stream(bytes, decoder, accumulator)` does the reading. It folds every slice that is ready into one result, so a burst of
reads costs one `result()` call, and it yields to the executor after a bounded number of slices so a source that is always
ready cannot starve painting or cancellation. A transport or decoding error ends the run, but content accumulated before
it is delivered first and stays on the message.

### Partial JSON

Tool arguments are JSON that arrives in fragments. A UI wants to show `{"city":"Oslo"` as it grows, but nothing may act on
it until it is complete. `ai-ui-stream::partial_json::Parser` keeps an incremental parse: after each `append` the
`snapshot()` holds the best reading so far, a `State` of `Partial` or `Complete`, and the path of the value still being
written. It enforces limits on bytes, nodes and depth.

```rust
use ai_ui_stream::partial_json::{Limits, Parser, State};

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let mut parser = Parser::new(Limits::default())?;
    for fragment in [r#"{"city":"Os"#, r#"lo","units":"#, r#""metric"}"#] {
        parser.append(fragment)?;
        let snapshot = parser.snapshot();
        let complete = snapshot.state == State::Complete;
        println!("{} (complete: {complete})", snapshot.value);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

```text
{"city":"Os"} (complete: false)
{"city":"Oslo"} (complete: false)
{"city":"Oslo","units":"metric"} (complete: true)
```

The accumulator keeps the raw argument text (`args_text`) separately from the parsed `args`, and the runtime runs a tool
only from complete arguments. A response that ends mid-arguments produces an error result for that call instead of
executing a repaired guess (see [Tools and approvals](02-concepts.md#tools-and-approvals)).

## Three wire formats

| Format | Marker | Framing | Decoder | Selected by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AI SDK UI message stream (v5 to v7) | `x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v1` | SSE, one JSON object per `data:` event, optional `[DONE]` | `UiMessageStreamDecoder` | `DataStreamAdapter` (default) |
| AI SDK data stream (v4) with assistant-ui's `aui-*` extensions | `x-vercel-ai-data-stream: v1` | `CODE:JSON` lines, no SSE | `DataStreamDecoder` | `DataStreamAdapter`, by header |
| assistant-transport (assistant-stream) | none | SSE, `data: <JSON>`, ends `data: [DONE]` | `SseDecoder`, `run_stream_from_sse` | your own adapter |

The UI message stream header is the same for AI SDK v5, v6 and v7, so it does not tell you the SDK version. The format is
a superset over time: newer versions add optional fields.

### The AI SDK UI message stream

Events are typed JSON objects: `start`, `text-start` / `text-delta` / `text-end` (with an `id`), the `reasoning-*`
equivalents, `tool-input-start` / `tool-input-delta` / `tool-input-available` / `tool-input-error`,
`tool-output-available` / `tool-output-error` / `tool-output-denied`, `tool-approval-request` / `tool-approval-response`,
`source-url`, `source-document`, `file`, `data-<name>`, `start-step`, `finish-step`, `reset-step`, `finish`, `abort`,
`error` and `message-metadata`. The decoder below feeds the bytes in 11-byte reads to show that framing does not matter:

```rust
use ai_ui_stream::{MessageAccumulator, StreamDecoder, UiMessageStreamDecoder};

fn text_of(result: &ai_ui_core::ChatModelRunResult) -> String {
    result
        .content
        .iter()
        .flatten()
        .filter_map(|part| match part {
            ai_ui_core::AssistantMessagePart::Text(t) => Some(t.text.as_str()),
            _ => None,
        })
        .collect()
}

fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let wire = concat!(
        "data: {\"type\":\"text-start\",\"id\":\"t1\"}\n\n",
        "data: {\"type\":\"text-delta\",\"id\":\"t1\",\"delta\":\"Hello, \"}\n\n",
        "data: {\"type\":\"text-delta\",\"id\":\"t1\",\"delta\":\"world\"}\n\n",
        "data: {\"type\":\"text-end\",\"id\":\"t1\"}\n\n",
        "data: {\"type\":\"finish\",\"finishReason\":\"stop\"}\n\n",
        "data: [DONE]\n\n",
    );
    let mut decoder = UiMessageStreamDecoder::default();
    let mut accumulator = MessageAccumulator::default();
    // Network reads can split anywhere, even inside a UTF-8 character.
    for read in wire.as_bytes().chunks(11) {
        for chunk in decoder.push(read)? {
            accumulator.push(chunk);
        }
        let result = accumulator.result();
        if !text_of(&result).is_empty() {
            println!(
                "{} -> {:?}",
                String::from_utf8_lossy(read).escape_debug(),
                text_of(&result)
            );
        }
    }
    for chunk in decoder.finish()? {
        accumulator.push(chunk);
    }
    accumulator.finish();
    println!("{:?}", accumulator.status());
    Ok(())
}
```

It prints the text as it grows (`Hello, `, then `Hello, world`) and ends with `Complete { reason: Stop }`. The same loop
with a tool call whose arguments stream in two pieces:

```rust
use ai_ui_stream::{MessageAccumulator, StreamDecoder, UiMessageStreamDecoder};

fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    // A tool call whose arguments stream in pieces, as a real model produces them.
    let wire = concat!(
        "data: {\"type\":\"tool-input-start\",\"toolCallId\":\"c1\",\"toolName\":\"get_weather\"}\n\n",
        "data: {\"type\":\"tool-input-delta\",\"toolCallId\":\"c1\",\"inputTextDelta\":\"{\\\"city\\\":\"}\n\n",
        "data: {\"type\":\"tool-input-delta\",\"toolCallId\":\"c1\",\"inputTextDelta\":\"\\\"Oslo\\\"}\"}\n\n",
        "data: {\"type\":\"tool-input-available\",\"toolCallId\":\"c1\",\"toolName\":\"get_weather\",\"input\":{\"city\":\"Oslo\"}}\n\n",
    );
    let mut decoder = UiMessageStreamDecoder::default();
    let mut accumulator = MessageAccumulator::default();
    for chunk in decoder.push(wire.as_bytes())? {
        accumulator.push(chunk);
    }
    for chunk in decoder.finish()? {
        accumulator.push(chunk);
    }
    for part in accumulator.parts() {
        if let Some(call) = part.as_tool_call() {
            println!(
                "{}: args_text={} args={}",
                call.tool_name,
                call.args_text,
                serde_json::Value::Object(call.args.clone())
            );
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

prints `get_weather: args_text={"city":"Oslo"} args={"city":"Oslo"}`. Note that, as in upstream's decoder, the UI-stream
decoder holds tool input back until `tool-input-available` and then writes it as one piece; the legacy data stream below
streams argument text progressively.

`ai-ui-stream` is deliberately lenient on this wire: content that arrived is kept, and a lifecycle violation such as a delta
before its start produces a warning, not a failed run. The strict reducer that mirrors AI SDK 7 error for error is a
separate crate, `ai-ui-sdk-stream`, described in [AI-SDK-STREAM](../AI-SDK-STREAM.md). For a valid stream both give the same
content; they differ only on malformed or unusual ones. Which events `ai-ui-stream` does not represent yet
(`reasoning-file`, `custom`, `steering-message`, citations, message metadata, tool `inputEncoding` and `title`, abort
reason) is tracked in [PROTOCOL](../PROTOCOL.md#conformance-status). Two deliberate improvements over assistant-ui's own
UI-stream adapter are worth knowing: `data-*` parts with an `id` replace the earlier part with that name and id, and
`reset-step` discards the parts of the current step.

### The data stream and the `aui-*` extensions

The older format is one `CODE:JSON` per line: `0` text, `g` reasoning, `b` / `c` / `9` tool input start, delta and complete
call, `a` tool result, `d` finish message, `e` finish step, `f` start step, `h` source, `k` file, `2` data, `8` annotations,
`3` error. assistant-ui adds codes of its own on the same framing: `aui-state` (state operations), `aui-text-delta`,
`aui-reasoning-delta`, `aui-data`, `aui-reasoning-part-start` and `aui-tool-call-approval`, and extends several stock codes
with fields such as `parentId`, `artifact`, `isPreliminary` and `modelContent`. `DataStreamDecoder` handles all of these. As
upstream's default decoder it is strict: a malformed value or a reference to an unknown tool call fails the stream.
The full code table is in [PROTOCOL](../PROTOCOL.md#a2-legacy-ai-sdk-data-stream-ai4319).

### assistant-transport

assistant-stream's own SSE format carries the chunk vocabulary almost directly: 13 event types, each with a numeric `path`
addressing a part (`part-start`, `text-delta`, `tool-call-approval`, `result`, `update-state`, and so on), ending with
`data: [DONE]`. Because it is not an AI SDK format, `DataStreamAdapter` does not select it. Wrap your response bytes with
`run_stream_from_sse` inside your own adapter:

```rust
use ai_ui_core::adapter::RunStream;
use ai_ui_core::{AppendMessage, ChatModelRunOptions, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime};
use ai_ui_stream::{run_stream_from_sse, MessageAccumulator};
use std::convert::Infallible;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll};

/// A response body that arrives in the given reads.
struct Reads(std::vec::IntoIter<Vec<u8>>);

impl futures_core::Stream for Reads {
    type Item = Result<Vec<u8>, Infallible>;
    fn poll_next(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, _cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Option<Self::Item>> {
        Poll::Ready(self.0.next().map(Ok))
    }
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // An assistant-transport response: part-start, text deltas addressed by part path, [DONE].
    let wire = concat!(
        "data: {\"type\":\"part-start\",\"part\":{\"type\":\"text\"},\"path\":[]}\n\n",
        "data: {\"type\":\"text-delta\",\"textDelta\":\"Served \",\"path\":[0]}\n\n",
        "data: {\"type\":\"text-delta\",\"textDelta\":\"by assistant-transport\",\"path\":[0]}\n\n",
        "data: [DONE]\n\n",
    );
    let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(
        move |_options: ChatModelRunOptions| -> RunStream {
            // In an app, `bytes` is the body of your own HTTP request.
            let bytes = Reads(
                wire.as_bytes()
                    .chunks(24)
                    .map(<[u8]>::to_vec)
                    .collect::<Vec<_>>()
                    .into_iter(),
            );
            run_stream_from_sse(bytes, MessageAccumulator::default())
        },
        LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
    );
    futures_executor::block_on(runtime.append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Hi"))?)?;
    println!("{}", runtime.messages()[1].text());
    println!("{:?}", runtime.messages()[1].status());
    Ok(())
}
```

Malformed or unknown events are dropped with a warning, as in assistant-stream. `update-state` carries state operations
(`set`, `append-text`) with string paths, which the accumulator applies to the message's `unstable_state` metadata. The
result is delivered to the next request as `state`. A runtime for assistant-transport with server-owned state is not
ported yet ([STATUS](../STATUS.md#not-yet-ported)).

## Requests: `ai-ui-data-stream`

`DataStreamAdapter<C: HttpClient>` is a `ChatModelAdapter`. For each model step it builds a JSON body, POSTs it, checks the
status, picks a decoder and returns the run stream. `request_body(options, extra)` is public if you need the same body in your
own transport. The body follows `useDataStreamRuntime`:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `messages` | The selected path plus the assistant message being continued, converted to model-style `role` / `content` messages (`to_model_messages`). |
| `system` | The system prompt, when the app set one. |
| `tools` | Tool name to `{ parameters, description }`. Schemas only; there is no `execute` on the wire. |
| `unstable_assistantMessageId` | The id of the assistant message being filled. |
| `threadId` | The thread's remote id, when it has one. |
| `parentId` | The id of the message being answered (`null` for the first). |
| `runConfig` | The run configuration, normally `{}`. |
| `state` | The message's `unstable_state`, when not null. |
| call settings and config | Flattened into the top level (for example `temperature`, `modelName`). |
| `DataStreamOptions::body` | Extra fields from your callback, applied last, so they can override anything above. |

`Content-Type: application/json` is always set; other headers come from `DataStreamOptions::headers`, a closure called per
request so a refreshed token is picked up. The conversion drops what a model request cannot carry (reasoning, sources,
timestamps) and gives an old tool call that never completed the error result `{"error":"Tool call was not completed"}`, as upstream does, instead of leaving it dangling.

```rust
use ai_ui_data_stream::{DataStreamOptions, Protocol};
use std::rc::Rc;

fn main() {
    let token = "secret-token".to_owned();
    let mut options = DataStreamOptions::new("https://example.com/api/chat");
    // Evaluated for every request, so a refreshed token is picked up.
    options.headers = Some(Rc::new(move || {
        vec![("Authorization".into(), format!("Bearer {token}"))]
    }));
    // Extra top-level body fields, given the thread's remote id when it has one.
    options.body = Some(Rc::new(|thread_id| {
        let mut extra = serde_json::Map::new();
        extra.insert("model".into(), "my-model".into());
        extra.insert("threadId".into(), thread_id.into());
        extra
    }));
    // Skip header detection when you know what the server sends.
    options.protocol = Some(Protocol::UiMessageStream);
    println!("{}", options.api);
}
```

### Errors

| What happens | What the thread shows |
|---|---|
| The request cannot be made (DNS, refused, TLS) | The `HttpError` text; the message becomes `incomplete/error`. |
| A non-2xx status | `RunError::Failed` with the text `Status 503`. The response body is not read into the message. |
| The stream is malformed or cut inside an event | The run fails; text received before the failure stays on the message. |
| An `error` event inside the stream | The message becomes `incomplete/error` with `{ code, message }` (and `severity` when valid) as detail; content so far stays. |
| `cancel_run`, or dropping the run future | `incomplete/cancelled`, text so far kept. |

`ThreadView` turns the stored error into a readable `MessageState::error`, and the run future returns the same `RunError`
to your executor.

## HTTP clients: `ai-ui-http`

`HttpClient` has one method, `post(request, signal) -> ResponseFuture`. Two implementations ship:

- **`NativeClient`** (not `wasm32`): `ureq` with rustls. Each request runs on its own worker thread, and the body is passed
  through a bounded queue (64 reads of up to 16 KiB), so a slow consumer slows reading instead of buffering the response.
  It returns non-2xx responses to the adapter instead of failing, which is how `Status 503` is reported. Use
  `NativeClient::with_agent(agent)` for proxies or timeouts, and keep `http_status_as_error(false)` on that agent.
- **`FetchClient`** (`wasm32`): browser `fetch` with `credentials: same-origin`; set `include_credentials` for cross-origin
  cookies. Dropping the response body cancels the reader and aborts the request.

A client that owns your auth, retries or a different TLS stack only has to implement the trait.

### Cancellation

`runtime.cancel_run()` (or `ThreadView::stop`, or the composer's cancel) fires the run's `AbortSignal`. The signal reaches
the client as the second argument of `post`. The runtime stops polling the adapter's stream immediately and marks the message
`incomplete/cancelled`, so the UI reacts at once even if the server keeps the connection open. The native worker thread stops
at its next read and when the consumer is gone; the browser client aborts the fetch. The test
`cancelling_stops_a_stream_the_server_keeps_open` in `crates/ai-ui-http/tests/native.rs` checks that a cancelled run ends in
under three seconds against a server that holds the connection for five.

## Connect a real backend

Step by step, for an AI SDK backend.

**1. The server.** Any server that accepts a JSON POST and answers with an AI SDK stream works. With the AI SDK it is
a handler that passes the body to `streamText` and returns the UI message stream. This is the shape of the repository's interop
server, `benchmarks/ai-sdk-stream/interop-server.mjs` (shortened here):

```js
const body = JSON.parse(await readBody(req));
const result = streamText({
  model,
  messages: body.messages,   // model-style messages, passed straight through
  system: body.system,
  tools,                     // your tools, with their own execute
});
const response = result.toUIMessageStreamResponse();
// copy response.status, response.headers and the streamed body to the client
```

Two details from [PROTOCOL](../PROTOCOL.md#b3-request-body-contract) matter. `messages` are model messages, so do not
run `convertToModelMessages` over them (that is for a client that posts UI messages). And AI SDK 7 rejects system-role
messages inside `messages` by default, which is why the system prompt travels as a top-level field. `tools` in the body
are schemas only; the backend decides whether to use them.

**2. The client.** Build a runtime whose adapter is `DataStreamAdapter`. This compiles; set `AI_UI_API` to run it against a
live endpoint.

```rust
use ai_ui_core::{AppendMessage, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime};
use ai_ui_data_stream::{DataStreamAdapter, DataStreamOptions};
use ai_ui_http::NativeClient;
use std::rc::Rc;

/// A runtime whose model is an AI SDK endpoint.
fn chat_runtime(api: &str, token: String) -> LocalThreadRuntime {
    let mut options = DataStreamOptions::new(api);
    options.headers = Some(Rc::new(move || {
        vec![("Authorization".into(), format!("Bearer {token}"))]
    }));
    LocalThreadRuntime::new(
        DataStreamAdapter::new(NativeClient::new(), options),
        LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
    )
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // Set AI_UI_API to a running endpoint to try it; without it the example only builds the runtime.
    let Ok(api) = std::env::var("AI_UI_API") else {
        println!("set AI_UI_API=http://localhost:3000/api/chat to send a message");
        return Ok(());
    };
    let runtime = chat_runtime(&api, std::env::var("AI_UI_TOKEN").unwrap_or_default());
    let run = runtime.append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Say hello in five words."))?;
    match futures_executor::block_on(run) {
        Ok(()) => println!("{}", runtime.messages().last().unwrap().text()),
        Err(error) => println!("run failed: {error}"),
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

In the example app the same thing is `--api URL`, with `--header NAME:VALUE` for credentials.

**3. What goes out.** A POST to the URL with `Content-Type: application/json` and a body like this (printed by the loopback
example below for the message "Hello"):

```json
{
  "messages": [{ "content": [{ "text": "Hello", "type": "text" }], "role": "user" }],
  "parentId": "1a1cb95041d-1",
  "runConfig": {},
  "tools": {},
  "unstable_assistantMessageId": "1a1cb95041d-2"
}
```

The ids come from the runtime's `ids` option and are only examples.

**4. What must come back.** Status 2xx, then a streamed body. With the AI SDK, the response carries
`x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v1` and a body of SSE events (`data: {...}` separated by a blank line). Without
that header the adapter assumes the UI message stream; set `DataStreamOptions::protocol` if you serve the data stream and
cannot send its `x-vercel-ai-data-stream: v1` header. Proxies must not buffer the response, or the reply arrives in one piece.

**5. Multi-step runs.** If the model calls a tool you registered with `execute`, the runtime runs it and sends a second request
whose `messages` end with the assistant's tool call and its result. A backend that already executed the tool itself (the
interop server does) sends the result in the same stream, and no second request is needed.

**6. Check it.** The repository's `crates/ai-ui-http/tests/interop_ai_sdk.rs` runs this exact path against a real AI SDK 7
server over a mock model, with reasoning, a streamed tool call executed by the server, a second step, and a follow-up turn.
It needs Node and `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in `benchmarks/ai-sdk-stream`. The result covers the AI SDK UI message stream
only; other backends, authentication and retries are not covered ([STATUS](../STATUS.md#interop-with-a-real-backend)).

## Testing without a network

Because the adapter only needs an `HttpClient`, a backend is easy to fake. This client records the request and answers with
a canned stream, split into 16-byte reads to exercise the decoder:

```rust
use ai_ui_core::{AbortSignal, AppendMessage, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime};
use ai_ui_data_stream::{
    ByteStream, DataStreamAdapter, DataStreamOptions, HttpClient, HttpRequest, HttpResponse,
    ResponseFuture,
};
use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::rc::Rc;

/// A client that never touches the network: it records the request and
/// answers with a canned AI SDK UI message stream, split into small reads.
#[derive(Clone, Default)]
struct Loopback {
    last_request: Rc<RefCell<Option<serde_json::Value>>>,
}

impl HttpClient for Loopback {
    fn post(&self, request: HttpRequest, _signal: AbortSignal) -> ResponseFuture {
        *self.last_request.borrow_mut() = serde_json::from_slice(&request.body).ok();
        let wire = concat!(
            "data: {\"type\":\"text-start\",\"id\":\"t\"}\n\n",
            "data: {\"type\":\"text-delta\",\"id\":\"t\",\"delta\":\"Hi there\"}\n\n",
            "data: {\"type\":\"finish\",\"finishReason\":\"stop\"}\n\n",
            "data: [DONE]\n\n",
        );
        let reads: Vec<Result<Vec<u8>, _>> =
            wire.as_bytes().chunks(16).map(|c| Ok(c.to_vec())).collect();
        let body: ByteStream = Box::pin(Reads(reads.into_iter()));
        Box::pin(std::future::ready(Ok(HttpResponse {
            status: 200,
            headers: vec![("x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream".into(), "v1".into())],
            body,
        })))
    }
}

struct Reads(std::vec::IntoIter<Result<Vec<u8>, ai_ui_data_stream::HttpError>>);
impl futures_core::Stream for Reads {
    type Item = Result<Vec<u8>, ai_ui_data_stream::HttpError>;
    fn poll_next(
        mut self: std::pin::Pin<&mut Self>,
        _cx: &mut std::task::Context<'_>,
    ) -> std::task::Poll<Option<Self::Item>> {
        std::task::Poll::Ready(self.0.next())
    }
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let client = Loopback::default();
    let seen = client.last_request.clone();
    let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(
        DataStreamAdapter::new(
            client,
            DataStreamOptions::new("http://backend.test/api/chat"),
        ),
        LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
    );
    futures_executor::block_on(runtime.append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Hello"))?)?;
    println!("{}", runtime.messages()[1].text());
    println!(
        "{}",
        serde_json::to_string_pretty(seen.borrow().as_ref().unwrap())?
    );
    Ok(())
}
```

It prints `Hi there` followed by the request body shown above. To test the real client, bind a `TcpListener` on
`127.0.0.1:0` and point `NativeClient` at it; the example below does so for the data stream protocol, and
`crates/ai-ui-http/tests/native.rs` also covers an error status and cancellation against a server that never closes:

```rust
use ai_ui_core::{AppendMessage, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime};
use ai_ui_data_stream::{DataStreamAdapter, DataStreamOptions};
use ai_ui_http::NativeClient;
use std::io::{BufRead, BufReader, Read, Write};
use std::net::TcpListener;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // A one-request HTTP server on a loopback port.
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
    let url = format!("http://{}/api/chat", listener.local_addr()?);
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        let (mut stream, _) = listener.accept().unwrap();
        let mut reader = BufReader::new(stream.try_clone().unwrap());
        let mut length = 0;
        loop {
            let mut line = String::new();
            reader.read_line(&mut line).unwrap();
            if let Some(v) = line.to_ascii_lowercase().strip_prefix("content-length:") {
                length = v.trim().parse().unwrap();
            }
            if line == "\r\n" {
                break;
            }
        }
        reader.read_exact(&mut vec![0; length]).unwrap();
        let body = "0:\"Hello from a socket\"\nd:{\"finishReason\":\"stop\"}\n";
        write!(
            stream,
            "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nx-vercel-ai-data-stream: v1\r\nContent-Length: {}\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n{body}",
            body.len()
        )
        .unwrap();
    });

    let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(
        DataStreamAdapter::new(NativeClient::new(), DataStreamOptions::new(url)),
        LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
    );
    futures_executor::block_on(runtime.append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Hi"))?)?;
    println!("{}", runtime.messages()[1].text());
    Ok(())
}
```

For decoder work, replay bytes in arbitrary partitions: `crates/ai-ui-stream/tests/fixtures/protocol-vectors.json` holds 96 wire
vectors from the protocol audit, and `crates/ai-ui-stream/tests/protocol_vectors.rs` and `ai_sdk_vectors.rs` run them. As of
2026-11-09 the status in [PROTOCOL](../PROTOCOL.md#conformance-status) was 22 of the 23 assistant-stream vectors run matching and 52 of
65 AI SDK vectors matching, with each of the 13 differences recorded with its reason. Those figures are a snapshot; the tests are
the current truth.

Next: [Building a UI with Slint](04-ui-slint.md) puts a thread on screen, and [Running on the web](05-web.md) covers the browser.
