# docs/guide/04-ui-slint.md

---
title: Building a UI with Slint
description: The Slint thread UI, the Markdown stack behind it, how the example binds them to a runtime, settings, scaling, keyboard and focus, renderers, and how to embed the thread in your own Slint app.
order: 4
section: Build
---

# Building a UI with Slint

**What this page gives you.** This page covers the Slint thread UI: the components in `ai-ui-slint`, the Markdown stack, how `examples/thread` binds them to a runtime, settings, scaling, keyboard and focus, renderers, and embedding the thread in your own Slint app.

The runtime crates know nothing about windows. The Slint UI is two layers on top of them:

- `crates/ai-ui-slint` is a Slint source library: the components, fonts, icons and the `AssistantTheme` global.
- `examples/thread` is a complete application that binds those components to a runtime through `ai-ui-state`. It is both the demo and the reference for how to write the binding.

The components are presentation only. They draw what the host gives them and report what the user did. The host owns the conversation, the clipboard, disclosure state and every effect. That split is what lets the same components sit on the local runtime, an external store, or a thread list.

## What is in `ai-ui-slint`

The Rust side of the crate is one function, `ai_ui_slint::ui_dir()`, which returns the folder holding `lib.slint`. It has no dependencies, no renderer and no runtime code. Everything else is `.slint` source under `crates/ai-ui-slint/ui/`. A consumer imports from `lib.slint` only; files under `components/` are internal and can change.

The main components, all exported from `lib.slint`:

| Component | What it does |
|---|---|
| `AssistantThread` | Scrolling list of `ChatRow` messages. Tracks whether the reader follows the bottom, exposes `scroll-to-bottom()`, forwards every message action. |
| `AssistantMessage` (internal) | One row: user or assistant bubble, parts, status line, the action bar (copy, edit, regenerate, feedback) and the branch picker. |
| `AssistantComposer` | The input. Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line, Escape stops a running reply. Optional attachments row. |
| `AssistantEditComposer` | Inline editor shown inside a message while it is being edited. |
| `AssistantReasoningPreview` | Reasoning text in a bounded, collapsible viewport. |
| `AssistantToolFallback` (internal) | The default disclosure for a tool call: arguments, optional detail and result as plain text, with optional copy buttons. |
| `AssistantApproval` | The prompt for a tool that needs approval, with the choices the runtime offers. |
| `AssistantBranchPicker` | Previous/next control with "n / m". Disabled while a run is active. |
| `AssistantMarkdown` | Renders Markdown blocks: paragraphs, headings, code with a copy button, tables, rules. |
| `AssistantSuggestions` | Up to four suggested prompts on an empty thread. |
| `AssistantThreadList` | The sidebar: New Thread row, search field, one row per thread with a running indicator, a menu (Rename, Archive, Delete) and inline rename. |
| `AssistantThreadSelector` | A compact dropdown over a string model, with keyboard navigation and typeahead. |
| `AssistantSettingsMenu` | The Settings row and popover: text size, reading width, theme. |
| `AssistantAttachmentList`, `AssistantAttachmentChip`, `AssistantSourceCard` | Attachment and source presentation. |
| `AssistantButton`, `AssistantIconButton`, `AssistantCopyButton`, `AssistantFeedback`, `AssistantScrollbar`, `AssistantTooltipContent` | Building blocks. |
| `AssistantPagedText`, `AssistantChunkedText` | Long text shown as bounded pages or measured chunks, so one huge message does not stall layout. |

The shared records live in `models.slint`: `ChatRow`, `ChatPart`, `ChatPartKind`, `MessageRole`, `ApprovalRequest`, `ApprovalChoice` and others. A row carries its parts, a status string and tone, a branch token with `branch-number` and `branch-count`, and flags such as `can-edit`, `can-regenerate`, `can-copy` and `copied`. Fonts are Inter (regular, medium, semibold) and IBM Plex Mono for code, registered by `theme.slint`, with their licences next to them.

## The Markdown stack

Markdown is the expensive part of a chat UI, so it is kept off the UI thread and out of the per-frame path.

1. **`ai-ui-markdown`** parses and projects. `parse` builds a bounded `Document`; `presentation::project` produces sanitized render blocks. Raw HTML, images and unsupported URLs become text, never executable content. It does no I/O and has hard limits (`MAX_SOURCE_BYTES`, `MAX_EVENTS`, `MAX_NESTING`, `MAX_OUTPUT_BYTES`) that fail with an error instead of truncating.
2. **Settled blocks and a live tail.** While a reply streams only its end can change. `split::StreamSplit` keeps the blocks before the last two as settled, so each is formatted once, and re-parses only the live tail on each update. Two blocks stay live because a half-typed line can be absorbed by the block before it a moment later. If the source contains a link reference or footnote definition, which can change earlier blocks, the splitter stops settling and treats the whole source as the tail. Finished text is always formatted in one piece, which is exact for every document.
3. **Worker pool.** On native targets `pool::CoordinatorPool` runs several `Coordinator`s, one worker thread each, sharded by key. A key always goes to the same shard, so only the newest source for it is kept while a parse runs, and older results are labelled as previews. The default is one worker per core, leaving one for the UI thread, between 1 and 8. Setting `AI_UI_MARKDOWN_WORKERS=1` in the example restores a single worker for comparisons.
4. **`ai-ui-markdown-slint`** is the UI-side adapter. Its `Factory` trait maps portable blocks into the record types your own `.slint` generates (Slint generates distinct types per application). `cache::Cache` and `streaming::StreamingCache` hold the formatted blocks on the UI thread. You call `observe_one(key, text, streaming)` when a text changes, `poll()` on a timer, `take_changed()` to learn which texts finished, and `view(key, source, streaming)` to get the blocks. While a newer source is still being formatted the previous formatting stays on screen, so streaming text never flashes back to plain text.

Markdown blocks carry no font sizes, which is why a text size change does not touch this stack (see Scaling below). In the browser there are no worker threads, so the same projection runs inline on the UI thread under a 4 ms budget per poll. See [Running on the web](05-web.md).

## How the example wires it

`examples/thread/src/app.rs` is the binding. The shape is short:

- A `ThreadView` from `ai-ui-state` turns any `ThreadRuntime` into `ThreadState`: an `Arc<MessageState>` per message plus run status. The example subscribes to the view and calls `App::sync` on every notification.
- The runtime keeps a bounded change journal (`MessageChanges`). The view reads it with its own cursor, so a notification costs work in proportion to what changed. If a view falls behind the journal it falls back to one full read.
- `sync` compares each message's `Arc` pointer with the pointer the row last showed. Only rows whose pointer changed are rebuilt. A rebuilt row reuses its parts model: `update_row` writes only the parts that differ into the existing `VecModel`, so Slint re-lays out those parts and not the whole message. Rows that no longer match the thread are removed, and a structural change also drops Markdown work for messages outside the newest window.
- The Markdown cache is keyed by message id and part index. `sync` declares changed texts newest first, so the visible end of the thread formats first, and a 1 ms timer polls for finished work and refreshes only the rows whose text completed.
- Window callbacks (`send`, `stop`, `switch-branch`, `regenerate`, `begin-edit`, `save-edit`, `toggle-part`, `resolve-approval`, `submit-feedback`, thread rename/archive/delete/search) forward to `ThreadView` and `ThreadList`. Expanded or collapsed state is owned by the host, so it survives Slint recycling rows.

## Settings

The sidebar footer has a Settings row. It opens a popover with three groups:

| Group | Options |
|---|---|
| Text size | Small (0.9), Default (1.0), Large (1.15), Extra large (1.3) |
| Reading width | Compact, Default, Wide, Extra wide, Full |
| Theme | System, Light, Dark |

Reading width sets the maximum width of the message column at text scale 1.0: Compact 576 px, Default 704, Wide 880, Extra wide 1100, and Full, which uses the whole main area with 40 px side padding. The pixel width is multiplied by the text scale so the line length in characters stays the same, and the layout clamps it to the available area. The theme defaults to dark. System follows the operating system.

In the popover, Up and Down (and Home and End) move a cursor, Enter or Space chooses, and Escape closes it and returns focus to the Settings row. The popover scrolls when the window is shorter than its content.

**Keyboard shortcuts.** Ctrl+= makes text larger by one step, Ctrl+- smaller, and Ctrl+0 resets to Default. Cmd works the same on macOS. They are caught by a `FocusScope` around the window, so they work from the composer. The plain `+` and `_` keys count too, so the shortcut works without holding Shift on layouts where `=` needs it. The steps stop at the ends.

**Saved file.** Native runs save settings to `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/ai-ui-example-thread/settings.json`, falling back to `~/.config/...` and then `%APPDATA%`. The file is small JSON:

```json
{
  "text_scale": 1.0,
  "reading_width": "default",
  "theme": "dark"
}
```

`reading_width` is one of `compact`, `default`, `wide`, `xwide`, `full`. Reading and writing never fail the app: a missing or malformed file means defaults, bad fields are ignored, numbers are clamped (0.75 to 2.0), and a failed write is ignored. Writes go through a temporary file that is renamed over the target. Screenshot and benchmark runs neither read nor write the file.

**Command-line flags** override the saved values for one run and do not save until you change something in the UI:

```sh
cargo run -p ai-ui-example-thread -- --theme light --text-scale 1.15 --reading-width wide
cargo run -p ai-ui-example-thread -- --light          # same as --theme light
cargo run -p ai-ui-example-thread -- --api https://example.com/api/chat
```

`--open-settings` opens the popover, which is useful with `--screenshot`. In the browser, the same options come from the page; see the web guide.

## Scaling

Text size is one property: `AssistantTheme.text-scale`, a global in `theme.slint`. Every font size in message text, Markdown, code, reasoning, tool calls, approvals, source and attachment cards, buttons, the branch picker, the action row and the composer multiplies by it. Icons in scaled rows scale with the text. `AssistantTheme.hit-scale` is `max(1, text-scale)`: hit targets grow with the text but never shrink below their normal size, which is 28 to 32 px.

Nothing on the Rust side re-runs when you change it. The host sets the property; Slint re-evaluates only the rows the `ListView` has instantiated. Markdown is not re-parsed because its blocks hold unsized styled text. The measurements are in [PERFORMANCE](../PERFORMANCE.md#settings-text-size-reading-width-theme), including the note that layout cost does not grow with thread length because only visible rows lay out.

In your own app, set the theme and scale the same way:

```rust,ignore
use slint::ComponentHandle;

let theme = ui.global::<AssistantTheme>();
theme.set_text_scale(1.15);
theme.set_follow_system(false);
theme.set_scheme(AssistantColorScheme::Light);
```

## Keyboard and focus

- **Composer.** Enter sends when no run is active; Shift+Enter inserts a newline. While a run is active Enter does nothing and inserts no newline. Escape stops the run.
- **Focus follows intent.** After switching threads, starting an edit, or pressing the scroll-to-bottom button, focus moves to the composer. A run that starts does not steal focus from the sidebar if the sidebar has it.
- **Focus rings are for the keyboard.** A click focuses a button without drawing a ring; Tab draws one, and a later click hides it again. Tests in `crates/ai-ui-slint/tests/focus_visible.rs` cover this.
- **Hit targets.** An icon button's pointer area reaches past its visual (a 32 px target around a 24 px icon), and actions that opt in ignore a fast double click.
- **Thread list.** Enter or Space activates a row or New Thread; inline rename takes Enter to commit and Escape to cancel.
- **Following the bottom.** `AssistantThread.following` turns off only when the user scrolls away from the end, and back on when they return within a few pixels. Streaming content grows under a reader who follows and stays put for one who does not.
- **Accessibility.** Controls carry accessible labels (for example "Message input", "Settings", "Copy message"), and the Settings row exposes a default action.

## Renderers

The example enables Slint's winit backend with two renderers: femtovg on wgpu for windows, and the software renderer for tests, screenshots and benchmarks.

- **GPU window.** `SLINT_BACKEND=winit-femtovg cargo run -p ai-ui-example-thread --features gpu-window`. The `gpu-window` feature makes `build.rs` embed fonts and images as files instead of pixels. GPU renderers draw any font size from the font file.
- **Software renderer.** The default build embeds resources for it. Offscreen `--screenshot out.png` and `--bench` use it. It draws glyphs pre-rendered at sizes it finds in the source, so `build.rs` sets `SLINT_FONT_SIZES` to the sizes the four text scales produce; without that a scaled size would snap to the nearest embedded one. This adds about 1.4 MB to the binary. Component tests in `ai-ui-slint` render offscreen with their own software platform.
- **Browser.** The web build uses the femtovg renderer on WebGL with winit on a canvas.

Software-renderer screenshots show layout, not GPU text or effects.

**The femtovg patch.** The workspace carries `patches/femtovg`, femtovg 0.27.0 with one upstream change backported by hand (femtovg #366, "Keep WGPU pipelines across flushes that don't use them"). Without it, a streaming chat whose frames differ in what they draw recompiled GPU pipelines every few frames. The patch applies through `[patch.crates-io]` in the workspace `Cargo.toml` and is meant to go away when Slint depends on femtovg 0.28 or later. An application outside this workspace must add the same entry; see [patches/README.md](../../patches/README.md) for the numbers and the removal condition.

## Embedding the thread in your own app

Use the same Slint version as the crates, `=1.18.1`.

```toml
[dependencies]
slint = { version = "=1.18.1", features = ["compat-1-18"] }
ai-ui-core = "0.1"
ai-ui-state = "0.1"
ai-ui-markdown-slint = "0.1"

[build-dependencies]
ai-ui-slint = "0.1"
slint-build = "=1.18.1"

# Until a Slint release uses femtovg 0.28: without it a streaming chat uses about twice the CPU with the
# FemtoVG-WGPU renderer (see patches/README.md).
[patch.crates-io]
femtovg = { git = "https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust" }
```

`build.rs` registers the library path (this is the example's build script, trimmed):

```rust,ignore
use std::collections::HashMap;

fn main() {
    let libraries = HashMap::from([("assistant".to_string(), ai_ui_slint::ui_dir())]);
    let config = slint_build::CompilerConfiguration::new().with_library_paths(libraries);
    slint_build::compile_with_config("ui/app.slint", config).unwrap();
}
```

Then import from `@assistant` in your `.slint`. Slint generates record types per application, so re-export the ones your Rust code needs:

```slint
import "@assistant/assets/Inter-Regular.ttf";
import "@assistant/assets/Inter-Medium.ttf";
import { AssistantTheme, AssistantThread, AssistantComposer, ChatRow } from "@assistant/lib.slint";
export { ChatRow, ChatPart, AssistantTheme, AssistantColorScheme } from "@assistant/lib.slint";

export component AppWindow inherits Window {
    default-font-family: "Inter";
    background: AssistantTheme.background;

    in property <[ChatRow]> messages;
    in property <bool> running;
    in property <int> thread-revision: 1;
    in-out property <string> draft;
    callback send(string) -> bool;
    callback stop();
    callback toggle-part(string, string);

    VerticalLayout {
        AssistantThread {
            vertical-stretch: 1;
            messages: root.messages;
            busy: root.running;
            conversation-revision: root.thread-revision;
            toggle-part(message-id, part-id) => { root.toggle-part(message-id, part-id); }
        }
        AssistantComposer {
            busy: root.running;
            draft <=> root.draft;
            submit(text) => { return root.send(text); }
        }
    }
}
```

On the Rust side, follow `examples/thread/src/app.rs`: build a `ThreadView` over your runtime, keep an `Rc<VecModel<ChatRow>>`, update it from a view subscription, and map the window callbacks to view actions. Give each Markdown text a key, feed changed texts to a `StreamingCache`, and poll it on a short timer.

Three rules from the components' own documentation matter when you write the host:

- Change `conversation-revision` whenever the selected conversation changes, even if the model is emptied and refilled in between.
- Every action that can have an effect (copy, open a source, retry an upload) is off by default. Turn on `can-copy-message`, `can-copy-code`, `can-open-source` and the like only when the host handles them, and revalidate the identifiers a callback carries before acting.
- Slint, which is not MIT, has its own licence terms: GPL-3.0, the Royalty-Free licence with an attribution badge, or a commercial licence. See [THIRD_PARTY.md](../../THIRD_PARTY.md).

Next: [Running on the web](05-web.md) for the WebAssembly build of this same example, and the [crate reference](06-crates.md) for the Rust side.

---

# docs/guide/05-web.md

---
title: Running on the web
description: Build the thread UI for WebAssembly, embed the demo in a page, and know what works in the browser and what does not.
order: 5
section: Build
---

# Running on the web

**What this page gives you.** This page covers the WebAssembly build: which crates run in the browser, the build command, embedding the demo in a page, the size of the output, and the known limits (WebGL required, small-text softness).

The runtime crates have no I/O, clock or thread dependencies, so they compile for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` unchanged. The Slint example also builds for the browser: the same `examples/thread` application, drawn with Slint's femtovg renderer on WebGL, with winit driving a `<canvas>`. The reference is [WEB.md](../WEB.md); this page explains it and adds the embedding details.

## What runs in the browser

| Piece | In the browser |
|---|---|
| `ai-ui-core`, `ai-ui-stream`, `ai-ui-sdk-stream`, `ai-ui-data-stream`, `ai-ui-state`, `ai-ui-markdown` | Yes. No I/O, clock or thread dependencies. |
| `ai-ui-http` | Yes. `FetchClient` (browser `fetch`) replaces `NativeClient` (ureq) on wasm32. |
| `ai-ui-clipboard` | Yes. `navigator.clipboard` on `wasm32-unknown-unknown`; arboard on desktop. |
| `ai-ui-markdown-slint`, `ai-ui-slint` | Through the example only. They are Slint crates with `publish = false`. |
| `examples/thread` | Yes, as the demo. |

Check any single crate with:

```sh
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p ai-ui-core
```

`scripts/gate.sh` builds the non-Slint crates for wasm32 as part of the full gate (`--quick` skips the wasm builds).

## Building the demo

`scripts/build-web-demo.sh` does the whole build. From a checkout:

```sh
scripts/build-web-demo.sh
```

It reads the `wasm-bindgen` version from `Cargo.lock` (`0.2.129`), finds the binary on `PATH` or in `WASM_BINDGEN`, and fails with a clear message if the two versions differ. Then it:

1. Runs `cargo build --locked --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p ai-ui-example-thread --features gpu-window`. The `gpu-window` feature makes the Slint build embed fonts and images as files, which the GPU renderer wants, instead of as pixels for the software renderer.
2. Runs `wasm-bindgen --target web --no-typescript --out-name ai_ui_example_thread` over the `.wasm`.
3. Writes `dist-web/ai-ui-web-demo.tar.gz` containing `ai_ui_example_thread.js`, `ai_ui_example_thread_bg.wasm` and `pixel-snap.js`, and `dist-web/ai-ui-web-demo.sha256`.

If `wasm-bindgen` is not on `PATH`:

```sh
WASM_BINDGEN=/path/to/wasm-bindgen scripts/build-web-demo.sh
```

The version must match exactly because the glue code and the `.wasm` are generated as a pair; a mismatch fails at load time with an unhelpful error, which is why the script checks first. Unpack the tarball next to your page:

```sh
mkdir -p public/wasm
tar -xzf dist-web/ai-ui-web-demo.tar.gz -C public/wasm
```

## Embedding the demo in a page

Serve the files and a page with a `<canvas>` inside a container that has a definite size. Slint's winit backend looks for a canvas with the id `canvas`, so give it that id. `pixel-snap.js` (in the tarball) lays the canvas out on whole device pixels; call it before `init()`:

```html
<div id="stage" style="width: 100%; height: 640px">
  <canvas id="canvas" tabindex="0"></canvas>
</div>
<script type="module">
  import { pixelSnap } from "./wasm/pixel-snap.js";
  import init from "./wasm/ai_ui_example_thread.js";
  pixelSnap(document.getElementById("canvas"));
  await init();
</script>
```

`tabindex="0"` lets the canvas take keyboard focus. The canvas fills its container's padding box, so size the container with CSS. Do not size the canvas itself; the helper does, and winit rewrites its inline size.

**Why the helper.** The canvas backing store is a whole number of device pixels, but a container that is centred, sized in `vh`, or shown on a 1.25x or 1.5x display makes the canvas box fractional. Firefox then resamples the canvas bilinearly and all text softens; Chrome snaps the box and hides it. The helper insets the canvas to whole device pixels so the two match 1:1. Details and measurements are in [WEB.md](../WEB.md).

### Passing options

The app reads the same options as the desktop command line, in either of two places, with the first taking priority:

- `window.__AUI_ARGS`, set before `init()` runs: `window.__AUI_ARGS = "history=1000&light"`.
- The page's query string: `?history=1000&light`.

Each `key=value` pair becomes `--key value`, and a bare `key` becomes `--key`. So `history=1000&light` is `--history 1000 --light`. Values are URL-decoded. Useful options in the browser:

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `history=N` | Start with a generated thread of N messages. |
| `light`, `theme=system\|light\|dark` | Theme. |
| `text-scale=1.15`, `reading-width=wide` | Text size and reading width for this session. |
| `long-reply-kb=9`, `token-delay-ms=4` | Shape of the demo model's replies. |

`--api` (an AI SDK endpoint) is not available in the browser build of the example. There is no settings file in the browser build, so settings last for the page session.

### Milestones on `window.__aui`

The demo publishes counters on `window.__aui`, which a page can poll:

- `frames`: number of frames drawn so far.
- `started`, `firstFrame`, `lastFrame`: `performance.now()` timestamps.
- `importMs` and `messages`, when a mock thread was loaded with `thread=URL`.

Panics are routed to `console.error`. `firstFrame` is the right signal for hiding a loading cover.

### Load on click

The WebAssembly file is large for a web page, so the landing site does not load it until the visitor asks. The pattern is small:

```ts
function hasWebGL(): boolean {
  try {
    const c = document.createElement("canvas");
    return !!(c.getContext("webgl2") || c.getContext("webgl"));
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}

async function load() {
  if (!hasWebGL()) { showMessage("This browser has no WebGL."); return; }
  window.__AUI_ARGS = "history=10000";
  const mod = await import(new URL("wasm/ai_ui_example_thread.js", document.baseURI).href);
  try {
    await mod.default();
  } catch (e) {
    // winit unwinds out of run() as control flow; anything else is a real failure.
    if (!/control flow/.test(String(e))) { showMessage(`Could not start: ${e}`); return; }
  }
  const wait = () => window.__aui?.firstFrame ? hideCover() : setTimeout(wait, 50);
  wait();
}
button.addEventListener("click", load);
```

Two details come from the landing site's implementation. First, hovering or focusing the button can add `<link rel="prefetch">` tags for the glue and the `.wasm`, so the files are in the cache when the click comes, and nothing is compiled until then. Second, winit's `run()` throws a "control flow" exception on purpose to hand control back to the browser's event loop. Treat that one as success.

## Size

From the landing site's measurement of the release build (`lto`, `opt-level` 3), taken 2026-11-11: the `.wasm` file is 9,500,548 bytes raw (9.06 MiB), 2.81 MiB with `gzip -9` and 1.91 MiB with brotli at quality 11. Serve it with gzip or brotli compression.

These three numbers are not in `docs/RESULTS.md` or `docs/WEB.md` on this branch. They are in `site/data/benchmarks.json` on the landing branch, which is the site's single source for figures. Re-measure after any dependency change; the file is dominated by Slint, femtovg and the embedded fonts.

## HTTP and clipboard in your own app

The example cannot call a backend in the browser, but your app can. `ai-ui-http::FetchClient` implements the `HttpClient` trait that `ai-ui-data-stream` uses, over `fetch` with `credentials: same-origin`. Set `include_credentials` for cross-origin cookies. Dropping the response body cancels the reader and aborts the request.

```rust,ignore
use ai_ui_core::{LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime};
use ai_ui_data_stream::{DataStreamAdapter, DataStreamOptions};
use ai_ui_http::FetchClient;

let adapter = DataStreamAdapter::new(
    FetchClient::default(),
    DataStreamOptions::new("/api/chat"),
);
let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(adapter, LocalRuntimeOptions::default());
```

The fetch client is exercised in headless Chromium by `crates/ai-ui-http/tests/browser/run.py`. It needs `wasm-bindgen` 0.2.129 (`WASM_BINDGEN`) and Playwright (`AI_UI_PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE`), and opens no window. `crates/ai-ui-clipboard/tests/browser/run.py` does the same for the clipboard.

`ai-ui-clipboard` reports the real outcome of a copy. Call `Clipboard::copy` synchronously inside the user gesture, for example a click handler, because browsers reject writes outside one. The API needs a secure context (HTTPS or `localhost`). One write may be pending at a time; a second returns `CopyError::Busy`.

## Limits

- **No Markdown worker threads.** Native builds format Markdown on a pool of worker threads. The browser build runs a wasm-only inline backend on the UI thread, with a 4 ms budget per poll and only the newest source per key. Long replies cost UI-thread time that native builds spend elsewhere.
- **Demo model only.** The example's browser build runs the built-in demo model. Use `FetchClient` with `ai-ui-data-stream` in your own app to reach a real backend.
- **HiDPI softness.** The canvas backing store follows `devicePixelRatio` (checked in Chrome at real scale factors 1.25, 1.5 and 2, see [WEB.md](../WEB.md)); Playwright's `deviceScaleFactor` emulation does not, so headless screenshots taken with it show a 1x canvas. A fractional canvas box softens text in Firefox unless you use `pixel-snap.js` (above). Small text, code blocks especially, can still look softer than DOM text on 1x displays because femtovg draws unhinted grayscale glyphs. Safari was not tested.
- **WebGL is expected.** The demo is built for the femtovg WebGL renderer, and the landing page refuses to start it in a browser without WebGL, hence the check above.
- **Frame rates in headless tests are a floor.** Headless Chromium uses software WebGL (SwiftShader), so a frame rate measured there is the GPU emulated on a busy CPU. Treat headless numbers as a floor, not as what a browser with a GPU gives, and do not compare them with native numbers.

## Cloudflare Pages notes

The landing site (`site/` on the landing branch, built with Astro) is configured for Cloudflare Pages; nothing is deployed from the repository.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Root directory | `site` |
| Build command | `npm ci && npm run build` |
| Build output directory | `dist` |

The Pages build image has no Rust toolchain. Build the wasm files first (`npm run wasm` in `site/`, which runs the cargo and `wasm-bindgen` steps and writes `public/wasm`), then run `npx wrangler pages deploy dist` from CI, or add the wasm step to a CI job that uploads `dist`. `public/_headers` sets `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` for `/wasm/*` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` for everything. A longer cache lifetime is safe only if the file names change with each build.

Next: the [crate reference](06-crates.md).

# Crate reference

**What this page gives you.** This page lists every crate in the workspace with its purpose, key types, features, wasm32 support, publishing status and a short example, plus a table for choosing which crates to depend on.

The workspace has ten library crates and one example application. Names below were checked against each crate's `lib.rs` and its compiled rustdoc. For the narrative, start with [Concepts](02-concepts.md); for the layering rationale, see [ARCHITECTURE](../ARCHITECTURE.md).

## Dependency graph

Built from the `Cargo.toml` files (an arrow points from a crate to a crate it depends on):

```mermaid
graph TD
  core[ai-ui-core]
  stream[ai-ui-stream]
  sdk[ai-ui-sdk-stream]
  data[ai-ui-data-stream]
  http[ai-ui-http]
  state[ai-ui-state]
  md[ai-ui-markdown]
  mdslint[ai-ui-markdown-slint]
  slint[ai-ui-slint]
  clip[ai-ui-clipboard]
  ex[examples/thread]

  stream --> core
  data --> core
  data --> stream
  http --> core
  http --> data
  state --> core
  mdslint --> md
  ex --> core
  ex --> state
  ex --> data
  ex --> http
  ex --> mdslint
  ex --> clip
  ex -. build .-> slint
  ex -. wasm32 only .-> md
```

`ai-ui-core`, `ai-ui-sdk-stream`, `ai-ui-markdown`, `ai-ui-clipboard` and `ai-ui-slint` depend on no other workspace crate. `ai-ui-sdk-stream` depends only on `serde_json`.

## Status at a glance

| Crate | wasm32 | Checked by | Publishing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ai-ui-core` | yes | gate, CI | on crates.io (0.1) |
| `ai-ui-stream` | yes | gate, CI | on crates.io (0.1) |
| `ai-ui-sdk-stream` | yes | gate, CI | on crates.io (0.1) |
| `ai-ui-data-stream` | yes | gate, CI | on crates.io (0.1) |
| `ai-ui-http` | yes (`FetchClient`) | gate, CI | on crates.io (0.1) |
| `ai-ui-state` | yes | gate, CI | on crates.io (0.1) |
| `ai-ui-markdown` | yes, without the thread-based modules | gate, CI | on crates.io (0.1) |
| `ai-ui-clipboard` | yes (`navigator.clipboard`) | gate (`scripts/gate.sh`) | on crates.io (0.1) |
| `ai-ui-markdown-slint` | only inside the example | demo build | on crates.io (0.1); needs the femtovg patch with FemtoVG-WGPU |
| `ai-ui-slint` | no Rust code to compile; Slint sources only | demo build | on crates.io (0.1); needs the femtovg patch with FemtoVG-WGPU |

"gate" means `scripts/gate.sh` builds the crate with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`. "CI" means the `wasm` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` does too; that job does not list `ai-ui-clipboard` today, the local gate does. The Slint crates reach wasm32 through `examples/thread`, which `scripts/build-web-demo.sh` builds ([web guide](05-web.md)).

None of the library crates defines Cargo features. Platform differences are `cfg(target_arch)` and `cfg(target_os)` switches, not flags. The only feature in the workspace is `gpu-window` on the example. This guide does not assume the crates are on crates.io; depend on them by path or Git.

Minimum Rust versions in the manifests: workspace default 1.85, `ai-ui-clipboard` 1.86, `ai-ui-markdown` 1.88, both Slint-facing crates 1.92.

## ai-ui-core

The Rust port of `@assistant-ui/core`: the message model, the branching message repository, the model adapter contract and the runtimes. Depends only on `serde`, `serde_json` and `futures-core`.

Key items:

- `ThreadMessage` (with `UserMessage`, `AssistantMessage`, `SystemMessage`) and the part types (`TextPart`, `ReasoningPart`, `ToolCallPart`, `SourcePart`, and so on). The JSON shape matches upstream, and fields the port does not model round-trip through `extra`.
- `MessageRepository`: the branch tree with a selected path, export/import and `MessageChanges`, the bounded journal views use to read only what changed.
- `ChatModelAdapter`: `fn run(&self, ChatModelRunOptions) -> RunStream`, a stream of cumulative `ChatModelRunResult`s. A closure with that signature works. `adapter::once` and `adapter::from_results` build streams for tests.
- `ThreadRuntime`: the trait UIs bind to. `LocalThreadRuntime` implements it with append, run loop, cancel, branches, tool results and human tools; `ExternalStoreRuntime` implements it over an `ExternalStore` you own.
- `ThreadList` with a `ThreadListAdapter`: list, rename, archive, delete, titles; optimistic changes roll back on failure.
- `SmoothText` / `SmoothOptions`: the smooth-streaming reveal.
- `AbortController` / `AbortSignal`, `Subscription` (drop to unsubscribe), `ToolRegistry` / `Tool`.

The runtime is single-threaded (`Rc`) and executor-agnostic: methods do their synchronous work at once and return a `RunFuture` that you spawn. There is no ambient clock or randomness, which is why the crate builds for wasm32.

```rust,ignore
use ai_ui_core::{adapter, AppendMessage, ChatModelRunResult, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime, ThreadRuntime};

let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(
    |_options| adapter::from_results([Ok(ChatModelRunResult::text("Hello!"))]),
    LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
);
let run = runtime.append(AppendMessage::user_text(None, "Hi")).unwrap();
futures_executor::block_on(run).unwrap();
assert_eq!(runtime.messages().last().unwrap().text(), "Hello!");
```

Compiled and run against this checkout by hand; the same example is a doctest in the crate.

## ai-ui-stream

The port of `assistant-stream`: typed chunks, the accumulator that folds them into an assistant message, partial JSON for tool arguments, and the `assistant-transport` SSE serialization. Depends on `ai-ui-core`.

Key items:

- `Chunk` / `ChunkKind` / `PartInit` / `FinishReason`: the typed stream events.
- `MessageAccumulator` (with `AccumulatorLimits`): `push(chunk)`, `result()` for the cumulative `ChatModelRunResult`, `finish()`, `status()`, `warnings()`.
- `StreamDecoder`: the trait a wire format implements. Provided: `SseDecoder` (assistant-transport), `DataStreamDecoder` (AI SDK data stream) and `UiMessageStreamDecoder` (AI SDK UI message stream).
- `run_stream` and `run_stream_from_sse`: turn a response byte stream into a `RunStream` for an adapter. Slices that are ready are folded into one result per wake-up.
- Modules `partial_json` and `state` (state operations) for the pieces behind it.

```rust,ignore
use ai_ui_stream::{run_stream_from_sse, MessageAccumulator};
use ai_ui_core::RunStream;

// `bytes` is any futures Stream of Result<Vec<u8>, E> where E: Display.
fn adapter_stream(bytes: impl futures_core::Stream<Item = Result<Vec<u8>, String>> + 'static) -> RunStream {
    run_stream_from_sse(bytes, MessageAccumulator::default())
}
```

Compiled against this checkout.

## ai-ui-sdk-stream

A bounded, incremental fold of the AI SDK 7 UI message stream (`x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v1`) into messages. It depends only on `serde_json`, forbids unsafe code, denies `unwrap`/`expect`/`panic` in its sources, and is checked by a differential test against the published AI SDK. The header names a wire format, not an SDK major version. Legacy data-stream and assistant-transport adapters are not part of this crate.

Key items:

- `Runtime`: the single-owner engine. `Runtime::new(message_id, Config)`, `ticket()`, `push(ticket, bytes, observe)`, `end(ticket)`, `cancel(ticket)`, `restart(message)`, `view()`.
- `RunTicket`: a run's identity. Feeding with a stale ticket returns `FeedOutcome::IgnoredStale` without parsing.
- `Delivery` and `MessageView`: what `push` hands your callback. The view is borrowed, so the ordinary delta path never clones the message; call `snapshot()` only when you need an owned JSON value.
- `Config` / `Limits` (`event_bytes`, `run_bytes`, `parts`), `UnknownPolicy`, `ServerErrorPolicy`.
- `UiReducer`, `Update`, `ApplyResult`, `StreamError`.

Limits are this crate's policy, not upstream protocol limits, and oversized input fails explicitly rather than truncating.

```rust,ignore
use ai_ui_sdk_stream::{Config, Runtime};

let mut runtime = Runtime::new("msg-1", Config::default()).unwrap();
let ticket = runtime.ticket();
let wire = b"data: {\"type\":\"start\",\"messageId\":\"msg-1\"}\n\n\
             data: {\"type\":\"text-start\",\"id\":\"t\"}\n\n\
             data: {\"type\":\"text-delta\",\"id\":\"t\",\"delta\":\"Hi\"}\n\n";
runtime
    .push(ticket, wire, |delivery| {
        let _parts = delivery.view.part_count();
    })
    .unwrap();
println!("{}", runtime.view().snapshot());
```

Compiled and run against this checkout; it prints a message with one streaming text part containing `Hi`.

## ai-ui-data-stream

The port of `@assistant-ui/react-data-stream`: a `ChatModelAdapter` for AI SDK backends. It sends upstream's request body and reads either a UI message stream or a data stream, detected from the AI SDK response headers. Depends on `ai-ui-core` and `ai-ui-stream`.

Key items:

- `DataStreamAdapter<C>` and `DataStreamOptions`: `DataStreamOptions::new(api)` with optional `headers` and `body` closures evaluated per request and an explicit `protocol`.
- `HttpClient`: one method, `post(HttpRequest, AbortSignal) -> ResponseFuture`. Implement it for your own HTTP stack.
- `HttpRequest`, `HttpResponse` (`header(name)`), `HttpError`, `ByteStream`.
- `Protocol` and `resolve_protocol`.
- `request_body`, `to_model_messages` and `to_language_model_messages`: the request-body pieces, public so you can build your own transport.

```rust,ignore
use ai_ui_core::{LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime};
use ai_ui_data_stream::{DataStreamAdapter, DataStreamOptions};

let adapter = DataStreamAdapter::new(my_http_client, DataStreamOptions::new("https://example.com/api/chat"));
let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(adapter, LocalRuntimeOptions::default());
```

The ready-made clients are in `ai-ui-http`; the example in the next section compiles.

## ai-ui-http

Ready-made `HttpClient` implementations. Depends on `ai-ui-core` and `ai-ui-data-stream`, plus target-specific dependencies: `ureq` with rustls off wasm32, and `wasm-bindgen`, `web-sys` and friends on wasm32.

Key items:

- `NativeClient` (not wasm32): `NativeClient::new()` or `NativeClient::with_agent(ureq::Agent)`. One worker thread per request.
- `FetchClient` (wasm32 only): browser `fetch`, `credentials: same-origin` by default, with `include_credentials: bool` for cross-origin cookies. Dropping the response body aborts the request.

The two never exist in the same build, so write code that picks the client with `cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")`.

```rust,ignore
use ai_ui_core::{LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime};
use ai_ui_data_stream::{DataStreamAdapter, DataStreamOptions};
use ai_ui_http::NativeClient;

let adapter = DataStreamAdapter::new(
    NativeClient::new(),
    DataStreamOptions::new("https://example.com/api/chat"),
);
let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(adapter, LocalRuntimeOptions::default());
```

Compiled against this checkout (it does not connect to anything). On wasm32, replace `NativeClient::new()` with `FetchClient::default()`. A Chromium smoke test (`crates/ai-ui-http/tests/browser/run.py`) exercises `FetchClient`.

## ai-ui-state

The UI-agnostic state layer, after upstream's scoped state. A UI renders `ThreadState` from a `ThreadView` and calls the view's actions, whatever toolkit it uses and whichever runtime sits below. Depends on `ai-ui-core`.

Key items:

- `ThreadView`: `new(runtime, ViewOptions)`, `for_list(&ThreadList, ..)`, `subscribe(callback)`, `state() -> Arc<ThreadState>`, `rebind(runtime)`, `tick(now_ms)` and `needs_frame()` for smooth-streaming animation.
- Actions on the view: `send`, `stop`, `reload`, `switch_branch`, `begin_edit`, `edit_composer`, `copy_text`, `mark_copied`, `toggle_part`, `respond_to_approval`, `add_tool_result`, `submit_feedback`.
- `ThreadState` (`messages: Vec<Arc<MessageState>>`, `is_empty`, `is_running`, `capabilities`) and `MessageState` with `PartState`.
- `PartKind`: `Text`, `Reasoning`, `ToolCall`, `Source`, `Image`, and the other part kinds.
- `ToolCallState`, `ToolStatus`, `ToolPresentation`, `ApprovalState`, `ApprovalDecision`.
- A row cache keyed by `Arc` identity: a message that did not change keeps its `Arc`, which is how the example decides which Slint rows to rebuild. The clock is supplied by the caller (`tick(now_ms)`, `mark_copied(id, now_ms)`).

```rust,ignore
use ai_ui_core::{adapter, ChatModelRunResult, LocalRuntimeOptions, LocalThreadRuntime};
use ai_ui_state::{ThreadView, ViewOptions};
use std::rc::Rc;

let runtime = LocalThreadRuntime::new(
    |_options| adapter::from_results([Ok(ChatModelRunResult::text("Hello!"))]),
    LocalRuntimeOptions::default(),
);
let view = ThreadView::new(Rc::new(runtime), ViewOptions { smooth: None });
let _subscription = view.subscribe(|| println!("changed"));
let run = view.send("Hi").unwrap().unwrap();
futures_executor::block_on(run).unwrap();
assert_eq!(view.state().messages.len(), 2);
```

Compiled and run against this checkout. Drop the returned `Subscription` to unsubscribe.

## ai-ui-markdown

The port of `@assistant-ui/markdown`: a bounded, safe parser and block projection for streaming chat text. Dependencies: `pulldown-cmark`, `url`, `serde`. It never fetches images, opens links, renders HTML or performs I/O; those are inert data, and links need an explicit host action.

Key items:

- `parse(source) -> Result<Document, ParseError>` with `Document`, `Block`, `Inline`, `Alignment`. Hard limits `MAX_SOURCE_BYTES` (1 MiB), `MAX_EVENTS`, `MAX_NESTING`, `MAX_OUTPUT_BYTES` fail with an error, never a silent truncation.
- `presentation::project(source)`: the UI-independent projection into `RenderBlock`s, plus `safe_destination` for link targets.
- `split::StreamSplit` and `split::top_level_blocks`: settled blocks versus the live tail for streaming text.
- `scheduling::Scheduler`: coalesces snapshots and tracks revisions.
- Native only: `coordinator::Coordinator` (a latest-snapshot worker), `pool::CoordinatorPool` (several coordinators sharded by key; `default_workers()`, at most `MAX_WORKERS` = 8) and `worker::Worker`.

On wasm32 the thread-based modules are compiled out; the browser demo runs `project` inline.

```rust,ignore
use ai_ui_markdown::{parse, split::StreamSplit};

let document = parse("# Title\n\nSome **bold** text.").unwrap();
assert_eq!(document.blocks.len(), 2);

// While text streams, settled blocks are formatted once and only the tail again.
let mut split = StreamSplit::new();
let (settled, tail) = split.update("one\n\ntwo\n\nthree\n\nfo");
println!("{} settled blocks, live tail {} bytes", settled.len(), tail.len());
```

Compiled and run against this checkout.

## ai-ui-markdown-slint

Converts the portable Markdown presentation into Slint records and manages the UI-thread cache. On crates.io (0.1). Depends on `ai-ui-markdown` and Slint (`=1.18.1`, default features off).

Key items:

- `Factory`: you implement `cell` and `block` to map the shared `Block<C>` / `BlockKind` / `Alignment` into the record types your own `.slint` generates.
- `convert` and `literal`: build blocks from a presentation, or from literal source with a warning when formatting is unavailable. Run them on the Slint thread.
- `cache::Cache`, `cache::Backend` (nonblocking executor contract), `cache::Limits`, `cache::NativeBackend` (a worker pool; not on wasm32).
- `streaming::StreamingCache<K, F, B>`: `observe_one(key, text, streaming)`, `poll()`, `take_changed()`, `view(key, source, streaming)`, `retain(keep)`, `has_pending()`. Each settled block is a cache entry of its own.

```rust,ignore
use ai_ui_markdown_slint::{cache::{Limits, NativeBackend}, streaming::StreamingCache};

let backend = NativeBackend::start(2048, 256 * 1024).ok();
let mut markdown = StreamingCache::new(
    MyFactory, // your `Factory` implementation
    backend,
    Limits { keys: 2048, presentation_units: 8 * 1024 * 1024 },
);
markdown.observe_one((message_id, part_index), &text, still_streaming);
// On a timer: if markdown.poll() { for key in markdown.take_changed() { /* refresh that row */ } }
```

Fenced as `ignore` because it needs your generated Slint types; `examples/thread/src/markdown.rs` is the compiling version.

## ai-ui-slint

The Slint component library: thread, messages, composer, branch picker, action bar, reasoning and tool disclosures, thread list, settings menu and Markdown blocks. On crates.io (0.1), no Cargo dependencies, `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. The Rust API is one function; everything else is `.slint` under `ui/`, listed in [Building a UI with Slint](04-ui-slint.md).

Key items:

- `ai_ui_slint::ui_dir() -> PathBuf`: the folder containing `lib.slint`, for the consuming build script. Use it at build time only.
- From `lib.slint`: `AssistantThread`, `AssistantComposer`, `AssistantMarkdown`, `AssistantThreadList`, `AssistantSettingsMenu`, `AssistantApproval`, `AssistantBranchPicker`, `AssistantTheme` and the records `ChatRow` and `ChatPart`.
- Its dev-dependency on Slint is for offscreen component tests; consumers pick their own backend and renderer.

```rust,ignore
// build.rs
let libraries = std::collections::HashMap::from([("assistant".to_string(), ai_ui_slint::ui_dir())]);
let config = slint_build::CompilerConfiguration::new().with_library_paths(libraries);
slint_build::compile_with_config("ui/app.slint", config).unwrap();
```

## ai-ui-clipboard

Host-owned clipboard text operations that report whether the copy worked. No Slint or conversation-state dependency. On Linux, Windows and macOS it uses `arboard` (with Wayland data control) on a bounded worker thread; on `wasm32-unknown-unknown` it uses `navigator.clipboard`.

Key items:

- `Clipboard::new()`, `copy(text, completion)`, `read_text(completion)`, `shutdown()`. Dropping the handle also shuts it down.
- `Completion`: a boxed `FnOnce(Result<(), CopyError>) + Send`. `ReadCompletion` is the same for reads.
- `CopyError`: `TooLarge`, `Unavailable`, `Busy`, `Rejected`, `Cancelled`, `WorkerStopped`. `ReadError` is its read counterpart. Errors never contain clipboard content.
- `MAX_COPY_BYTES` (1 MiB) and `MAX_READ_BYTES` (4 MiB).

On native, the completion runs on the worker, so dispatch UI updates back to the UI thread. In the browser, call `copy` synchronously inside the user gesture.

```rust,ignore
use ai_ui_clipboard::{Clipboard, CopyError};

if let Ok(clipboard) = Clipboard::new() {
    let _ = clipboard.copy(
        "hello".to_string(),
        Box::new(|result: Result<(), CopyError>| {
            if let Err(error) = result {
                eprintln!("copy failed: {error}");
            }
        }),
    );
}
```

Compiled against this checkout (not run: running it writes to the system clipboard).

## Choosing crates

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| A runtime and tools, no UI | `ai-ui-core` |
| A backend that speaks the AI SDK protocols | `ai-ui-core` + `ai-ui-data-stream` + `ai-ui-http` |
| A custom transport | `ai-ui-core` + `ai-ui-stream` (assistant-transport) or `ai-ui-sdk-stream` (AI SDK 7 UI messages, standalone) |
| State for your own UI toolkit | the above + `ai-ui-state` |
| Markdown in your own renderer | `ai-ui-markdown` |
| The Slint thread UI | all of the above + `ai-ui-markdown-slint` + `ai-ui-slint`; see [the Slint guide](04-ui-slint.md) |

Next: [Performance](07-performance.md) for the measured results, or [Coming from assistant-ui](08-from-assistant-ui.md) for the parity table.
