# docs/guide/07-performance.md

---
title: Performance
description: Why ai-ui is fast, the measured results against upstream assistant-ui, and how to reproduce every number.
order: 7
section: Reference
---

# Performance

**What this page gives you.** This page explains where the cost goes, with file names; gives the measured results against upstream assistant-ui with their conditions; lists what was not measured and what was corrected; and gives the commands to reproduce every figure.

This page has two parts. The first explains the design decisions behind the speed, with the files that hold them.
The second gives the measurements, how to read them, what they do not cover and how to reproduce them. Every figure
comes from [RESULTS](../RESULTS.md) (generated from [`results.json`](../results.json)). The engineering record,
including rejected experiments, is [PERFORMANCE](../PERFORMANCE.md).

## Why it is fast

A streaming chat does the same small thing many times: a few bytes arrive, one message grows, one row on screen
changes. A slow chat redoes work proportional to the whole thread for each of those events. Most of the design is
about making the cost of one event independent of everything else in the thread.

### One streamed update costs the same at any thread length

The repository behind every runtime (`crates/ai-ui-core/src/repository.rs`) keeps a bounded change journal: the last
64 content revisions, stored as the indices of the selected-path messages that changed, not as copies of message
bodies. Each `ThreadView` (`crates/ai-ui-state/src/view.rs`) owns its own cursor, so one consumer never consumes
another's changes. When the cursor is current and the thread's shape is unchanged, the view projects only the rows
that changed. If the cursor is missing or expired, or the structure changed (an edit, a branch switch, a new
message), the view falls back to a full projection. Correctness never depends on the journal.

The second half is `ThreadRuntime::structure_version`. While the tree's shape is unchanged, the view reuses branch
positions instead of looking each message up again, and patches its state and the repository's selected path in place
when nobody else holds a reference (`Arc::get_mut`). Retained snapshots stay immutable; copying them costs more, and
the code never mutates through a shared pointer.

The effect, from the 2026-11-10 record in PERFORMANCE: with smooth streaming on, one streamed update through runtime
and projection went from 8.5 to 1.7 microseconds at 1,000 existing messages and from 38.4 to 4.7 microseconds at
5,000 (median of five interleaved pairs). With 10 messages it did not change. That is a runtime-plus-projection
workload, not frame latency.

### Row sync touches only changed rows

The Slint side does not rebuild the list when a reply grows. The example host compares row identities (messages are
`Arc`, so identity is a pointer comparison) and updates changed rows and their part models in place. Streaming text
goes into one in-place row model per document. Animators for smooth streaming exist only for parts that are
streaming. The example's `App::sync` still compares identities across the selected thread; PERFORMANCE lists that as a
remaining cost.

### Markdown runs off the UI thread

`ai-ui-markdown` formats on a pool of worker threads (`crates/ai-ui-markdown/src/pool.rs`): one per core minus one for
the UI, between 1 and 8. Several coordinators sit behind one API, and a key always maps to the same shard. Each
shard keeps one parse in flight and only the newest source for a key. An older completion is labelled a preview, so
the UI keeps showing formatted text while newer text is pending instead of flashing plain text. The Slint cache
(`crates/ai-ui-markdown-slint/src/cache.rs`) is told which parts are visible, in priority order, so the parts the
person can see are submitted first. The browser build has no threads and runs a wasm-only inline backend instead.

### Settled blocks are formatted once, plus a live tail

Streaming Markdown is not re-parsed from the start on every delta. `StreamSplit` (`split.rs`) cuts the text into
settled blocks and a live tail; `StreamingCache` formats each settled block once and re-formats only the tail on each
frame. The result is tested to be equivalent to formatting the whole document, over every prefix of five documents.

### Long reasoning text is chunked

Reasoning can run to tens of kilobytes. The example (`examples/thread/src/chunks.rs`) shows it as chunks that are
appended once and never re-wrapped, with each chunk's height held in a property so the layout reads a cached value.
Layout and paint per frame at the end of a 40 KB reasoning stream went from 5.7 ms to 2.3 ms, and stayed flat over
the stream. Collapsed reasoning is not converted at all.

### Cheap decoding and fair scheduling

Complete SSE lines borrow the incoming bytes. Fragmented lines reuse a scratch buffer. The assistant-transport decoder
moves its JSON tree into typed deserialization instead of cloning it. The stream's 64-read budget now yields even for
heartbeat-only reads, so a fast stream cannot starve input and painting. Cumulative snapshots are coalesced; protocol
events never are. On the recorded workload (10,000 deltas, 240,000 bytes), the UI-message decoder plus accumulator
took 4.7 ms instead of 8.0 ms with 4 KB reads.

### A femtovg pipeline-cache patch

In a real GPU window, femtovg 0.27 dropped every cached render pipeline that a flush did not use, so a streaming
chat recompiled pipelines every few frames (about 70% of the main thread). The repository carries upstream's fix as
a patch in `patches/femtovg` (see `patches/README.md`). Process CPU in a 30 s run fell from 23.1-25.5 s to
11.8-14.1 s, and the median frame rate rose from 105-108 to 141-142 fps, the display's limit. An app that embeds the
Slint crates adds the same `[patch.crates-io]` entry until Slint ships femtovg 0.28.

### The list and large messages

The thread is a Slint `ListView`, so layout and paint cost follows the rows on screen. PERFORMANCE records that
changing text scale or reading width with 20,000 messages costs a few milliseconds of layout, and that the cost does
not grow with thread length because only visible rows relayout. STATUS still lists row instantiation across the whole
thread as a known remaining cost, so this guide does not claim a fully virtualised model.

A user message over 64 KiB or with at least 1,000 newlines is shown one verbatim page at a time (at most 16 KiB and
400 newlines; `examples/thread/src/paging.rs`). The runtime still holds the whole message, and copy, edit and model
requests use the full source. In a same-window layout microbenchmark with a 32,742-byte message, first layout and
paint took 9.589 ms raw against 5.554 ms paged. That is a layout figure, not a whole-application one.

### Memory

The Rust side keeps parsed text once and instantiates Slint rows. Resident memory in the like-for-like runs was
30 MiB at 1,000 messages and 64 MiB at 10,000 (table below). In the larger Rust-only runs, RESULTS records 166 MiB at
5,000 long structured messages and 552 MiB at 20,000 (117.9 MB of text, one run). Memory grows with the thread, as it must,
but slowly compared with a DOM.

One experiment was tried and reverted: one list row per Markdown block. It stayed within noise in rendering and
increased application work, because every update re-compared the blocks. The measurement is in PERFORMANCE.

## The measurements

Workload: upstream's thread (`@assistant-ui/react` 0.15.33 with plain CSS, in headless Chromium) against
`ai-ui-example-thread --bench N --bench-reply-kb K --bench-render` (offscreen, software raster, at most 60 frames a
second). The same history, the same demo reply (reasoning, then the answer, one word every 18 ms) and the same 60 s
window on both sides. Each cell is the median of 5 interleaved Rust and React pairs, release build, run on
2026-11-11, machine load about 4-6. Ranges are the minimum to maximum over the five runs. Ratios are the median
React value divided by the median Rust value, floored to one decimal.

### 1,000 messages, 9 KB prompt

| Measure | Rust | React | Ratio | Range of ratio | RESULTS row |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open the thread, like for like | 105.3 ms (100.8-150.9) | 2940 ms (2794-2987) | 27.9x | 18.5x-29.6x | 15 |
| CPU while streaming, 60 s | 17160 ms (13700-17650) | 73260 ms (73050-73540) | 4.2x | 4.1x-5.3x | 18 |
| Memory at the end, RSS | 30.1 MiB (29.7-30.4) | 1481.5 MiB (1474.5-1526.6) | 49.2x | 48.5x-51.4x | 11 |
| Memory at the end, Rust RSS vs React PSS | 30.1 MiB | 850.3 MiB (841.8-895.4) | 28.2x | 27.6x-30.1x | 14 |
| Longest iteration or frame while streaming | 34 ms (17.5-35.4) | 916.6 ms (866.6-1183.3) | 26.9x | 24.4x-67.6x | 7 |

### 200 messages, 40 KB prompt

| Measure | Rust | React | Ratio | Range of ratio | RESULTS row |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open the thread, like for like | 33.2 ms (31.8-46.6) | 1104 ms (1029-1197) | 33.2x | 22x-37.6x | 13 |
| CPU while streaming, 60 s | 17020 ms (13660-19450) | 51160 ms (41900-57120) | 3x | 2.1x-4.1x | 19 |
| Memory at the end, RSS | 24.6 MiB (24.5-24.8) | 1212.7 MiB (1210-1268) | 49.2x | 48.7x-51.7x | 10 |
| Memory at the end, Rust RSS vs React PSS | 24.6 MiB | 584 MiB (582.4-640.9) | 23.7x | 23.4x-26.1x | 16 |
| Longest stall | 109.9 ms (36.2-136.2) | 2399.9 ms (2183.2-2649.9) | 21.8x | 16x-73.2x | 5 |

### 10,000 messages, 9 KB prompt

| Measure | Rust | React | Ratio | Range of ratio | RESULTS row |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open the thread, like for like | 435.5 ms (382.9-472.1) | 26081 ms (23591-27196) | 59.8x | 49.9x-71x | 6 |
| CPU while streaming, 60 s | 22800 ms (20930-23220) | 83500 ms (76060-84710) | 3.6x | 3.2x-4x | 20 |
| Memory at the end, RSS | 63.6 MiB (63.3-64) | 3717.8 MiB (3675.4-3926) | 58.4x | 57.4x-62x | 8 |
| Memory at the end, Rust RSS vs React PSS | 63.6 MiB | 3088.9 MiB (3051.1-3298.6) | 48.5x | 47.6x-52.1x | 9 |
| Longest stall | 41.1 ms (28.3-46) | 11599.5 ms (9833-12899.5) | 282.2x | 213.7x-455.8x | 1 |

Source for all rows: `benchmarks/results/like-for-like/raw`, a release build of 424a4fb plus the open reporting of
that change. The summary script is `benchmarks/results/like-for-like/summarize.py`.

### Second run

A second, independent run of the 1,000-message comparison (2026-11-11, 9 interleaved pairs, release build, machine load
about 3-5 against 4-6 for the first run). Raw files and commands: `benchmarks/results/like-for-like-run2/`. The first run's
table above is unchanged; the full rows are in RESULTS (rows marked "run 2").

| Measure | Rust | React | Ratio | Range of ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open the thread, like for like | 97.5 ms (85.7-213.2) | 2472 ms (1870-2874) | 25.3x | 8.7x-33.5x |
| Longest iteration or frame | 16.68 ms (11.73-30.53) | 550 ms (416.6-983.3) | 32.9x | 13.6x-83.8x |
| Memory at the end, Rust RSS vs React PSS | 30.1 MiB (29.8-30.2) | 888 MiB (793.2-1066.3) | 29.5x | 26.2x-35.7x |
| Memory at the end, RSS | 30.1 MiB (29.8-30.2) | 1531.5 MiB (1427.7-1708.5) | 50.8x | 47.2x-57.3x |
| CPU while streaming, 60 s | 9690 ms (7570-14990) | 69360 ms (68190-73360) | 7.1x | 4.5x-9.6x |

The runs differ because of machine load: Rust's CPU was 17.2 s in run 1 and 9.7 s in run 2 (ratio 4.2x against 7.1x). CPU is
load-sensitive and is not a headline figure. Open, stall and memory agreed within the ranges.

Larger fixtures were measured earlier (2026-11-10, 3 interleaved pairs, load 6-25, long structured replies):

| Workload | Measure | Rust | React | Ratio | RESULTS row |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2,000 messages (12.2 MB) | open the thread | 527.1 ms (485.5-528.3) | 42090 ms (42090-96584) | 79.8x | 2 |
| 2,000 messages | longest iteration or frame | 41.5 ms (35-74.8) | 1633.2 ms (1633.2-4583.1) | 39.3x | 4 |
| 2,000 messages | resident memory | 88.1 MiB | 2946.3 MiB (2946.3-3449.1) | 33.4x | 12 |
| 2,000 messages | process CPU, 60 s | 9130 ms | 60260 ms | 6.6x | 17 |
| 5,000 messages (29.7 MB) | open the thread | 1256.7 ms (807.3-1256.7) | at least 120000 ms | at least 95.4x | 3 |

Two cautions apply to these. For 2,000 messages, one of three React runs did not finish opening within the harness's
120 s limit and is excluded, which understates React. For 5,000 messages React did not finish in 3 of 3 runs, so
120 s is a floor, not a measurement, and the ratio is a lower bound. Those older runs also used a harness that
measured React's open without checking the Markdown, which if anything understates React.

Rust against its own earlier state (not a React comparison): in a real GPU window, 1,000 messages, 30 s, process CPU
fell from 23.1-25.5 s to 11.8-14.1 s (1.8x, RESULTS rust-only row 1) and the median frame rate rose from 105 to 141 fps
(1.3x, row 2) after the femtovg patch.

## How to read these numbers

**What "open" means.** On the Rust side it is the time from the start of the history import until the last message's
Markdown is formatted and painted at least once: import, first sync, formatting on the worker threads, and a forced
frame. On the React side it is navigation until all messages are in the DOM with their Markdown rendered (every
reply's table present), plus two frames. Rust's first sync alone, when rows are on screen but Markdown is not yet
formatted, was 12.9 ms at 1,000 messages. It is a different, earlier event and is not compared with React.

**RSS and PSS.** RSS counts every resident page of a process, so summing it over Chromium's nine processes counts
shared pages several times. PSS divides shared pages among the processes that map them. The PSS ratio is therefore the
conservative memory comparison (28.2x against 49.2x at 1,000 messages). Rust runs as one process, where RSS is
the right figure.

**Medians and ranges.** Each value is the median of 5 interleaved runs. A range is the minimum to maximum of the
runs. The extremes of a ratio pair the best Rust run with the worst React run, so a wide ratio range is a statement
about noise, not a claim. The "longest stall" rows are single events and are the noisiest.

**A shared, busy machine.** The machine has 12 cores, is shared, and ran at load 4-6 for the like-for-like runs. Runs
are interleaved (Rust, React, Rust, React...) so load hits both sides alike. Absolute times move between days; only
the ratios and ranges are meaningful.

**Different clocks, same workload.** Rust's "longest stall" is the longest loop iteration, unpaced. React's is the
longest animation-frame interval. Rust's figures include software rasterisation on the CPU. React's CPU is the whole
Chromium process tree, including its own raster and compositing. React's main-thread busy time does not count raster
threads, which favours React. The React thread uses plain CSS and does somewhat less than upstream's default
Tailwind and Radix thread, which also favours React.

**Where React won.** No case was found on these workloads where React wins or ties.

## What we did not measure

- Any product other than upstream assistant-ui. This guide makes no comparison with others.
- React in a real GPU window. The harness cannot open one, so there is no GPU Rust-against-React ratio; the GPU rows
  are Rust against its earlier self.
- Long fixtures re-run with raw files kept: the 2,000- and 5,000-message rows come from 3 pairs on a loaded machine
  and have not been repeated at 5 pairs. React at 20,000 messages was started and interrupted.
- Fast-scroll frame time and composer typing latency with React. They were smoke-tested on Rust only and are not in
  the comparison tables.
- Memory growth over a five-minute stream.
- Retina or other high-DPI displays, and hardware other than the one machine above.
- Network and model latency. The demo reply is local; nothing here says how quickly a backend answers.

## Correction history

An earlier README and RESULTS headlined opening a 1,000-message thread at 0.12 s for Rust, against 2.9 s for React
(24x). The Rust figure was the time before Markdown had been formatted; the React figure ended with Markdown
rendered, so the comparison was not like for like. It was corrected on 2026-11-11. The measured like-for-like
ratio at 1,000 messages is 27.9x (18.5x to 29.6x), reflecting formatting that had since been cut from 0.52 s to
0.09-0.11 s by the worker pool. The 2026-11-10 values for 1,000 and 200 messages were also withdrawn, because their
raw files were not kept; the table above replaces them.

## Reproduce it yourself

The Rust side needs a release build; the React side needs Node and a headless Chromium. From the repository root:

```sh
cargo build --release -p ai-ui-example-thread
cd benchmarks/react-baseline
npm ci --ignore-scripts && npm run build
export PLAYWRIGHT=/path/to/node_modules/playwright   # any Playwright package
export CHROME=/path/to/chrome-headless-shell          # if Playwright's browser is not installed
node bench.mjs 1000 9 60        # one React run: 1000 messages, 9 KB prompt, 60 s; JSON on stdout
./compare.sh 1000 9 5           # five interleaved Rust and React pairs; raw output on stdout
```

The Rust half of one pair is `target/release/ai-ui-example-thread --bench 1000 --bench-reply-kb 9 --bench-render`.
To keep one file per run with the load average, use `benchmarks/results/run-pairs.sh stream 1000 9 5 OUT` with
`RUST_BIN`, `REACT_BASELINE`, `PLAYWRIGHT` and `CHROME` set (the script header lists them), then summarise with
`python3 benchmarks/results/like-for-like/summarize.py`. `python3 scripts/results.py check` verifies that RESULTS.md
and `results.json` agree.

To judge a Rust change against another revision, build both and alternate them:

```sh
scripts/ab-bench.sh BASE_REV NEW_REV 5 > ab.txt     # NEW_REV may be WORKTREE for uncommitted changes
```

It runs three scenarios (1,000 messages with render, 1,000 without, 200 messages with a 40 KB reply with render)
interleaved. Compare medians of p95, total and iterations over 4 ms, and keep the change only if nothing regresses.
The Rust-only decode and projection benchmarks are the ignored tests listed in PERFORMANCE, for example
`cargo test --locked --release -p ai-ui-state --test perf projection_cost_per_streamed_update -- --ignored --nocapture`.
Do not run them while compiling or while another benchmark is running.

Next: [Coming from assistant-ui](08-from-assistant-ui.md) for the parity table, or [Contributing and testing](09-contributing.md) for the gate and the A/B method.

---

# docs/guide/08-from-assistant-ui.md

---
title: Coming from assistant-ui
description: What is ported from assistant-ui, how packages map to crates, where the Rust API differs, and what is not there yet.
order: 8
section: Reference
---

# Coming from assistant-ui

**What this page gives you.** This page maps assistant-ui packages to crates, lists what is not ported, shows where the Rust API differs from the TypeScript one, states what a backend needs, and ends with a migration checklist.

ai-ui follows upstream's architecture module for module. The reference is assistant-ui commit `eb65bd4` (MIT). A
feature counts as ported when it behaves as upstream does, checked by tests derived from upstream's. The
authoritative list is [STATUS](../STATUS.md); this page organises it for someone who knows the TypeScript packages.

## Package to crate map

| Upstream | Crate | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `@assistant-ui/core` types and `MessageRepository` | `ai-ui-core` | Ported. Same JSON shape; unknown fields round-trip. |
| `ChatModelAdapter`, local thread runtime | `ai-ui-core` | Ported: append, edit, regenerate, branches, cancel, tool-result continuation, `maxSteps`, human tools, feedback, export and import. |
| Thread and edit composers | `ai-ui-core` | Ported: send, cancel, edit branching. No attachment adapter or dictation. |
| `useExternalStoreRuntime` | `ai-ui-core` | Ported. App-owned messages with edit, reload, cancel, tool and feedback callbacks; `Arc` identity kept for unchanged messages. |
| Thread list, `useRemoteThreadListRuntime` | `ai-ui-core` (`ThreadList`) | Ported: switch, new, rename, archive, unarchive, delete, generated titles, load; optimistic with rollback. The host supplies the `Spawner`. |
| `assistant-stream` (chunks, accumulator, state operations, partial JSON, assistant-transport SSE) | `ai-ui-stream` | Ported. Timing metadata is not computed. |
| AI SDK UI message stream and data stream | `ai-ui-stream` | Both protocols, including assistant-ui's `aui-*` data-stream extensions. |
| AI SDK `readUIMessageStream` | `ai-ui-sdk-stream` | A separate strict AI SDK 7 reducer, checked against the published package. |
| `@assistant-ui/react-data-stream` | `ai-ui-data-stream` | Ported: request conversion, protocol detection, error statuses (without the response text). |
| `fetch` in upstream | `ai-ui-http` | Native (ureq and rustls) and browser `fetch` clients. |
| `useSmooth` | `ai-ui-core` (`SmoothText`) | Same pacing as upstream. |
| Frontend tools and approvals | `ai-ui-core` (`Tool`, `ToolRegistry`) | Ported with approvals; tools run sequentially. |
| Scoped state (`MessageState`, `ThreadState`, `ComposerState`) | `ai-ui-state` | `ThreadView`, a UI-agnostic projection with scoped actions. |
| `@assistant-ui/react` thread look | `ai-ui-slint` | Thread, messages, composer, suggestions, reasoning and tool disclosure, branch picker, copy, edit, regenerate and feedback actions. |
| `@assistant-ui/markdown` | `ai-ui-markdown`, `ai-ui-markdown-slint` | Parsed off the UI thread; settled blocks plus a live tail. |
| Clipboard (browser API) | `ai-ui-clipboard` | Reports whether the copy actually worked, on native and in the browser. |

## What is not ported yet

These gaps are listed in STATUS, not hidden:

- **Runtimes.** assistant-transport (server-owned state) as a runtime; a concrete HTTP remote thread-list adapter;
  LangGraph and other framework adapters. The assistant-transport wire format is decoded; what is missing is the
  runtime that owns state on the server.
- **Generative UI.** Custom per-tool components. Tools render through a generic disclosure by default, and an app
  can register a presenter per tool (`ThreadView::set_tool_presenter`) to choose the title, summary and status. A
  custom Slint component per tool is not available.
- **Attachments.** Composer attachments with an adapter, and quotes.
- **Dictation and speech.** No speech or dictation adapters.
- **Other adapters.** Feedback, suggestion and history adapters, and the message queue.
- **Look.** The Slint UI follows upstream's default thread; Markdown styling fidelity in a real GPU window is marked
  unverified in STATUS, because offscreen screenshots use the software renderer.

## Where the Rust API differs

**No React hooks.** Upstream exposes state through hooks that re-render components. Here `ai-ui-state::ThreadView`
wraps any `ThreadRuntime`, projects it into plain data (message rows, parts, `isLast`, branch number and count,
`isCopied`, composer state) and offers the scoped actions. A UI subscribes, reads the view, and updates its own
widgets. The Slint example does this; another toolkit can too. `ThreadView` replaces `useThread`, `useMessage`
and `useComposer`.

**One runtime trait.** `ThreadRuntime` is a trait. The local runtime, the external-store runtime and thread-list
threads implement it, so the same UI works with all of them.

**Ownership, not ambient state.** Messages are immutable snapshots held in `Arc`. The view keeps a row cache keyed by
`Arc` identity, so an unchanged message is a pointer comparison and not a deep compare. An external-store app that
re-sends an unchanged message keeps its `Arc` and costs nothing downstream. Errors are `Result`s, not exceptions.

**No executor of its own.** Runtime methods do their synchronous work at once (the user message and the running
assistant message appear immediately) and return a future that you spawn: `slint::spawn_local`, a Tokio `LocalSet`,
or `wasm-bindgen-futures`. The runtime is single-threaded (`Rc`), like upstream's. Messages are `Arc` so adapters can
move them to worker threads. Do not wrap it in locks to make it look concurrent.

**No ambient clock or randomness.** Timestamps and ids come from options, and `ThreadView` takes a caller-supplied
clock for smooth streaming. That is what lets the core compile for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. `createdAt` is epoch
milliseconds.

**Subscriptions** are callbacks with a guard that unsubscribes when dropped, called after each state change and never
while internal state is borrowed.

**`AbortSignal`** becomes `ai-ui-core::abort`, a thread-safe signal an adapter can await or poll.

**Streaming adapters.** `ChatModelAdapter::run` returns a stream of cumulative `ChatModelRunResult`s, as upstream
does. A single result is a one-item stream. `run_stream` folds all slices that are ready into one result per wake-up.

## What a backend needs

Nothing new. The port reads and writes the wire protocols upstream's clients use: the AI SDK UI message stream, the
AI SDK data stream with assistant-ui's extensions, and the assistant-transport SSE format. A backend that serves
assistant-ui over these needs no change. A real AI SDK 7 `streamText` server over a mock model is exercised end to end
by `crates/ai-ui-http/tests/interop_ai_sdk.rs`: reasoning, a server tool call, a second step, and a follow-up turn
that replays the tool call. Not covered: other backends, authentication and retries. Details are in
[Streaming and backends](03-streaming-and-backends.md).

## Migration checklist

1. Pick the runtime: `LocalThreadRuntime` with a `ChatModelAdapter` (for example `ai-ui-data-stream` against your AI
   SDK endpoint), or `ExternalStoreRuntime` if your app owns the messages.
2. Replace hook calls with a `ThreadView` over that runtime, and call its actions where you called the hook's.
3. Spawn the futures the runtime returns on your executor.
4. Convert message storage, if any. The JSON shape is upstream's, so exported threads import without a mapping.
5. Re-create tools as `Tool` values with `execute`, or mark them `requires_approval`. Replace custom tool
   components with a presenter, or accept the generic disclosure.
6. Replace anything that used attachments, dictation or assistant-transport-as-runtime. These are the gaps above.
7. For a thread list, implement `ThreadListAdapter` and supply the `Spawner`.
8. Check wasm if you target the web: `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -p <crate>`.

## Licence of the toolkit

The Slint crates need a Slint licence of your choice; the runtime crates do not depend on Slint. See
[Building a UI with Slint](04-ui-slint.md) and [FAQ](10-faq.md).

Next: [Contributing and testing](09-contributing.md), or the [FAQ](10-faq.md) for short answers.

---

# docs/guide/09-contributing.md

---
title: Contributing and testing
description: Repository layout, prerequisites, the gate, tests, the benchmark method, and the conventions for code, docs and licences.
order: 9
section: Reference
---

# Contributing and testing

**What this page gives you.** This page covers the repository layout, prerequisites, the gate (`scripts/gate.sh`), the tests, the benchmark and A/B method, how to add a crate, and the documentation and licence conventions.

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md) and [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md) first. This page expands them.
Behaviour follows upstream assistant-ui, and gaps are listed in [STATUS](../STATUS.md) rather than implied.

## Repository layout

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `crates/` | Ten crates: `ai-ui-core`, `-stream`, `-sdk-stream`, `-data-stream`, `-http`, `-state`, `-markdown`, `-clipboard`, and the Slint crates `ai-ui-markdown-slint` and `ai-ui-slint` |
| `examples/thread` | The demo app and the host of the Slint components; also the web demo and the `--bench` harness |
| `benchmarks/` | `react-baseline`, `ai-sdk-stream` (AI SDK oracle), `upstream-look`, `results` (scripts behind `docs/results.json`), `performance-2026-11-10` (raw samples) |
| `docs/` | Reference documents, the guide in `docs/guide/`, and `results.json` |
| `scripts/` | `gate.sh`, `ab-bench.sh`, `build-web-demo.sh`, `results.py`, `check-guide.py` |
| `patches/` | The carried femtovg patch, described in `patches/README.md` |

Ownership by crate is in AGENTS.md: the core stays free of UI, I/O, ambient clocks and randomness; `ai-ui-sdk-stream`
is a separate strict reducer that you should not casually merge with the compatibility-oriented decoder in
`ai-ui-stream`; application-specific caching and paging belong in the host, not the components.

## Prerequisites

- **Rust.** The workspace `rust-version` is 1.85. A few crates need more, because their locked dependencies do:
  1.86 for `ai-ui-clipboard`, 1.88 for `ai-ui-markdown`, 1.92 for `ai-ui-slint` and `ai-ui-markdown-slint`. Do not
  raise a version to make a convenience API compile.
- **fontconfig headers** for the Slint crates: `libfontconfig1-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu. If `pkg-config` cannot find
  them, point `PKG_CONFIG_PATH` at the directory holding `fontconfig.pc`. Without the headers, build only the
  toolkit-independent crates: `-p ai-ui-core -p ai-ui-stream -p ai-ui-data-stream -p ai-ui-http -p ai-ui-state
  -p ai-ui-markdown`.
- **wasm.** `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Browser tests and the web demo need `wasm-bindgen` 0.2.129,
  the version in `Cargo.lock`; set `WASM_BINDGEN=/path/to/wasm-bindgen` if it is not on `PATH`.
- **Node** for the AI SDK interop check (`benchmarks/ai-sdk-stream`) and the React baseline.
- **Chromium** for the browser tests: set `AI_UI_PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE` and, optionally, `AI_UI_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE`.

## The gate

`scripts/gate.sh` runs the same checks CI runs, in this order:

1. `cargo fmt --all --check`
2. `cargo clippy --locked ... --all-targets -- -D warnings`
3. `cargo doc --locked --no-deps` on the runtime crates, with `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings"`
4. The AI SDK interop check: `npm ci --ignore-scripts` and `npm run verify` in `benchmarks/ai-sdk-stream`, then
   `AI_UI_REQUIRE_INTEROP=1` so a skipped interop test fails
5. `cargo build --locked --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` for the non-Slint crates
6. `cargo test --locked`

`scripts/gate.sh --quick` limits the scope to the runtime crates and skips the interop and wasm steps; it needs no
fontconfig headers or Node. Run the full gate before you propose a change that touches the Slint crates, wasm or
a wire protocol.

## Tests

- **Ported behaviour.** Derive tests from upstream's for each module you port, and add a test for every behaviour
  change.
- **Headless Slint window tests.** The Slint crates test components in offscreen windows
  (`crates/ai-ui-slint/tests/`, for example `action_bar.rs`, `composer_keys.rs`, `paged_text.rs`). They need no
  display. Render behaviour changes in an offscreen test and look at the image. The software renderer draws styled
  text as plain characters, so it does not establish Markdown styling fidelity; check that in a real window with
  `--features gpu-window`.
- **Browser tests.** `crates/ai-ui-clipboard/tests/browser` and `crates/ai-ui-http/tests/browser` run headless Chromium
  through `run.py` against a wasm build.
- **Interop.** `crates/ai-ui-http/tests/interop_ai_sdk.rs` runs against a real AI SDK 7 server over a mock model.
- **Debug builds are not for timing.** They include repository invariant walks.
- **Test status (2026-11-11, origin/main c2beb60).** Three consecutive full workspace runs (`cargo test --workspace --offline --release`): 334 passed, 0 failed, 7 ignored each time, no flaky tests observed. The ignored tests are 5 perf benchmarks, 1 example test and 1 doc test.

## Benchmark method

A change that claims to be faster must be measured, and the measurement must be reproducible:

- Use release builds, the same toolchain, workload and profile for both revisions.
- Warm up, then alternate the two builds (A, B, A, B...) with `scripts/ab-bench.sh BASE_REV NEW_REV [PAIRS]`. Do not
  compile or run other benchmarks at the same time.
- Report medians and ranges, keep the raw samples, and separate decoding, snapshots, projection, layout and paint, and
  whole-process CPU. A faster parser is not a frame measurement.
- The development machine is shared and busy (load 4-25 in recorded runs). Absolute numbers move; ratios from
  interleaved pairs are what count. Say so in the write-up.
- **Rule: results are published only if they were measured and can be reproduced.** Put the command and the raw files
  in the repository, record rejected experiments next to accepted ones in [PERFORMANCE](../PERFORMANCE.md), and add
  comparisons against upstream to `docs/results.json`. `python3 scripts/results.py render` rewrites the tables in
  RESULTS.md and floors every ratio to one decimal; `check` fails if the page and the JSON disagree.
- Do not add machine-specific compiler flags, `unsafe` code or dependencies without evidence that the bottleneck
  warrants them.

## Adding a crate or a feature

1. A new crate goes in `crates/<name>` (the workspace takes `crates/*`). Inherit `edition`, `license` and
   `rust-version` from the workspace, and give it a one-line `description`. Mark it `publish = false` if it depends on
   Slint.
2. Decide whether it must build for wasm. If so, add it to `RUNTIME` and `WASM` in `scripts/gate.sh` and to the CI
   package set, and keep it free of threads, clocks and file I/O.
3. If its dependencies need a newer Rust than 1.85, declare that in the crate's `rust-version`, and expect CI to check
   it with that exact toolchain.
4. Port the matching upstream tests. Record anything left out in STATUS.
5. Update the crate table in [Crate reference](06-crates.md), and [Coming from assistant-ui](08-from-assistant-ui.md)
   if it changes parity.
6. For a runtime feature that is hot, check the contracts in AGENTS.md: the bounded change journal, in-place updates
   only when a snapshot is uniquely held, and the 64-read yield in the stream scheduler.

## Documentation conventions

Every guide page is plain Markdown with front matter: `title`, `description` (one sentence), `order` (the number in the
file name) and `section` (Start, Build or Reference). The rules in the [guide index](README.md) apply:

- Performance numbers come only from `docs/RESULTS.md` or `docs/results.json`, with their conditions. Never mix a
  Rust time before Markdown formatting with a React fully rendered time.
- Compare only with upstream assistant-ui. State limits. No hype words, no emoji.
- Code must match the APIs in this repository. A snippet not compiled by tests is fenced as `rust,ignore`.
- Run `python3 scripts/check-guide.py` before you commit. It checks front matter, that the order matches the file
  name, and that every relative link resolves.

## Licensing

The project's own code is MIT (`LICENSE`). Portions are ported from assistant-ui (MIT, AgentbaseAI Inc.); keep the
notice in `NOTICE`, and mark new files that derive from upstream as ported from it. Bundled fonts, icons and
adapted code (Inter and IBM Plex Mono under the SIL Open Font License, Lucide icons under ISC, one file adapted from
the Vercel AI SDK under Apache-2.0) are listed in `THIRD_PARTY.md` with their licences beside the files. Add an entry
there when you bring in third-party material. Slint is GPL-3.0, royalty-free with an attribution badge, or commercial;
only the Slint crates and the example depend on it.

## CI policy

The gate is what counts, and it runs locally or on self-hosted machines. The project does not depend on paid, hosted
CI runners. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` mirrors the gate for whoever runs it, and PERFORMANCE records that a hosted
run on 2026-11-10 failed before any step started, which is why local results are what a change is judged on.
Report what you ran (the commands and the test counts) in your pull request.

Next: the [FAQ](10-faq.md), or [STATUS](../STATUS.md) for what is ported and what is not.

---

# docs/guide/10-faq.md

---
title: FAQ
description: Short answers to the questions people ask first about ai-ui, the Rust port of assistant-ui.
order: 10
section: Reference
---

# FAQ

**What this page gives you.** This page gives short answers to the questions people ask first, each with a pointer to the page or file that holds the detail.

## Is it production ready?

No. The repository describes itself as early (0.1). The runtime, the wire-protocol decoders and the Slint
thread are tested, and the gate (formatting, Clippy, documentation, tests, wasm builds, AI SDK interop) passes
locally. But it is a young port with listed gaps (see "What is not supported yet"), Markdown styling in a real GPU
window is marked unverified in [STATUS](../STATUS.md), and nothing is released. Evaluate it against your own needs
before you depend on it.

## Why Rust?

So that the same chat runtime can run in a native app and in WebAssembly, without a JavaScript engine in the
native case, and with predictable cost per streamed update. The core is free of UI, I/O, clocks and randomness, so
it compiles for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. Where this shows up in speed is described in [Performance](07-performance.md).

## Why Slint?

Slint is the toolkit the bundled UI uses: it runs on native desktops and in the browser, and its software renderer
makes headless tests possible. It is a choice for the UI crates only. The runtime crates (`ai-ui-core`, `-stream`,
`-data-stream`, `-http`, `-state`, `-markdown`, `-clipboard`) do not depend on Slint.

## Does it work with my backend or the AI SDK?

If your backend already serves assistant-ui, yes without changes: the crates read the AI SDK UI message stream, the AI
SDK data stream with assistant-ui's extensions, and the assistant-transport SSE format. The integration test runs a
real AI SDK 7 `streamText` server over a mock model, covering reasoning, a server tool call, a second step and a
follow-up turn. Other backends, authentication and retries are not covered by that test. See
[Streaming and backends](03-streaming-and-backends.md).

## Can I use it on the web, and how big is it?

Yes. `examples/thread` builds for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` (`scripts/build-web-demo.sh`) and runs on a canvas with
Slint's femtovg renderer on WebGL. Browser `fetch` and the clipboard are supported. Limits: no Markdown worker threads
(Markdown is formatted inline on the UI thread), the demo runs only the built-in demo model, and small text,
especially code, can look softer than DOM text on 1x displays, and a fractional canvas box softens text in Firefox
unless the page uses the bundled `pixel-snap.js`. The guide does not state a size for the bundle, because no size is recorded in
the repository's reference documents. Build it and measure `dist-web/`. See [Running on the web](05-web.md).

## How does it compare with assistant-ui in speed, and what is the catch?

On the recorded workloads, Rust opened a 1,000-message thread, Markdown formatted and painted, in 105 ms against
2.94 s for React (27.9x), used 17.2 s of CPU against 73.3 s for 60 s of streaming (4.2x), and 30 MiB of memory
against 1481 MiB RSS or 850 MiB PSS. Those are medians of 5 interleaved pairs on 2026-11-11; across all four runs that day the ratios were 16.6x to 27.9x for open, 23.8x to 42.7x for the longest stall, 28.2x to 35.4x for memory and 4.2x to 14.0x for CPU ([RUNS](../RUNS.md)).

The catch: the comparison is against upstream's thread with plain CSS in headless Chromium on a shared, busy machine;
the Rust side was offscreen with software raster; it was one machine; no GPU window was compared; and the 2026-11-10
numbers had to be corrected. Read "How to read these numbers" in [Performance](07-performance.md).

## Is it on crates.io?

Yes, all ten library crates, version 0.1: the eight toolkit-independent ones (`ai-ui-core`, `ai-ui-stream`,
`ai-ui-data-stream`, `ai-ui-sdk-stream`, `ai-ui-http`, `ai-ui-state`, `ai-ui-markdown`, `ai-ui-clipboard`) and the two
Slint crates (`ai-ui-slint`, `ai-ui-markdown-slint`). With Slint's FemtoVG-WGPU renderer, add the one-line femtovg patch
from the README until a Slint release includes the fix. The example app is not published.

## Which licence?

The project's own code is MIT, with portions ported from assistant-ui (MIT). Slint, used by the UI crates, is
available under GPL-3.0, a royalty-free licence that requires an attribution badge, or a commercial licence. An app
using the Slint crates must comply with the one it picks. Details are in `THIRD_PARTY.md` and `NOTICE`.

## Can I use my own UI toolkit with the runtime crates?

Yes. `ai-ui-core` and `ai-ui-state` do not depend on a toolkit. `ThreadView` projects any `ThreadRuntime` into plain
data and actions; a UI subscribes to it and updates its widgets. The Slint crates are one consumer. See
[Coming from assistant-ui](08-from-assistant-ui.md) for how `ThreadView` replaces React hooks.

## How do branches, edit and regenerate work?

As in upstream. `MessageRepository` is a tree of messages with a selected path. Editing a user message creates a
sibling branch; regenerating an assistant message does the same. The branch picker shows the current branch number and
count (`ThreadView` exposes both) and selects between siblings. Thread export and import use upstream's JSON shape.

## How do I stream tool calls?

Tool calls arrive as parts of the streamed assistant message, with their arguments filled in incrementally (partial
JSON is repaired as it grows). A `Tool` with `execute` runs in your app after each model step and its result feeds the
next step, up to `maxSteps`. A tool with `requires_approval` pauses the run until you call
`respond_to_tool_approval`. Tools run sequentially. A tool executed by the server arrives already resolved in the
stream. See [Concepts](02-concepts.md).

## What is not supported yet?

Assistant-transport as a runtime (the format is decoded), a concrete HTTP remote thread-list adapter, LangGraph and
other framework adapters, custom per-tool components (generative UI), attachment, speech, dictation, suggestion and
history adapters, the message queue, and composer attachments and quotes. The full list is in
[Coming from assistant-ui](08-from-assistant-ui.md) and [STATUS](../STATUS.md).

## How do I reproduce the benchmarks?

Build `ai-ui-example-thread` in release, build `benchmarks/react-baseline` with `npm ci --ignore-scripts && npm run
build`, set `PLAYWRIGHT` and `CHROME`, then run `./compare.sh 1000 9 5` from that directory. Raw per-run files and
the summary scripts are described in [Performance](07-performance.md#reproduce-it-yourself). `python3
scripts/results.py check` confirms that [RESULTS](../RESULTS.md) matches `docs/results.json`.

## Do numbers in this guide come from somewhere I can check?

Yes. Every figure is copied from `docs/RESULTS.md` or `docs/results.json` with its conditions. If a figure is not
there, the guide does not state it, which is why there is no bundle size above.

## How do I contribute?

Run `scripts/gate.sh`, port tests from upstream for behaviour changes, and publish results only when they are measured
and reproducible. See [Contributing and testing](09-contributing.md).

## Who maintains it?

The repository is under the GitHub account `iyiolacak`; the licence names "The assistant-ui Rust port contributors".
It is not affiliated with the assistant-ui or Vercel AI SDK projects. `SECURITY.md` says the private security contact
will be set when the repository is published.

Next: [Why ai-ui](00-why-ai-ui.md) for the summary, or [Getting started](01-getting-started.md) to try it.

---

# skills/ai-ui/SKILL.md

---
name: ai-ui
description: ai-ui is a Rust port of assistant-ui (crates.io, version 0.1): a chat runtime with branching threads, tools and approvals, decoders for the AI SDK UI message stream and data stream, bounded streaming Markdown, and an optional Slint chat UI, for native and WebAssembly apps. Use this skill when a user wants to add a chat runtime, AI SDK streaming, Markdown for streamed replies or a Slint chat UI to a Rust app, connect a Vercel AI SDK backend from Rust, port an assistant-ui React app to Rust, or debug the ai-ui-* crates. Triggers - ai-ui, assistant-ui in Rust, Slint chat UI, AI SDK stream in Rust, Vercel AI SDK backend from Rust, ai-ui-core, ThreadView.
---

# ai-ui

ai-ui is a Rust port of [assistant-ui](https://github.com/assistant-ui/assistant-ui). Ten library crates, all 0.1 on crates.io, plus `examples/thread`, a complete Slint app. It is early software and not affiliated with the assistant-ui or Vercel AI SDK projects.

Do not guess APIs. Read the reference files linked at the end, and the guides they point to, before writing code.

## Pick a mode

Choose from the user's request.

**Do the work.** The user wants ai-ui added, wired or fixed.
1. Inspect the project (Step 1) and report what you found and which crates you plan to add.
2. If the user asked to confirm first, stop and wait. Otherwise continue.
3. Implement in small steps. Prefer code copied from the guides and `examples/thread` over new code.
4. Verify (see the checklist) and report.

**Discuss or plan only.** The user asks whether it fits, what it would take, or for a plan. Make no file edits and run no `cargo add`. Read the project, then cover: fit, which crates, how it plugs into their executor and UI, the Slint and licence choices, known limits, and a numbered step plan. Wait for a go-ahead.

If the request is unclear, treat it as discuss mode and ask.

## Step 1: inspect the project

Report these before editing anything:
- Is it a Rust crate or a workspace? Which edition and Rust version (`rustc --version`, `rust-version` in Cargo.toml)?
- Which async runtime drives futures: Tokio, the Slint event loop, `wasm-bindgen-futures`, or none?
- Which UI toolkit, if any? Is Slint already used, and at which version?
- Does it target `wasm32-unknown-unknown`?
- Is there an AI SDK (Vercel) backend endpoint? What URL, and how does it authenticate?
- Does the project need a system prompt, tools or approvals?

## Pick crates

Add only what is needed, with `cargo add`.

| Need | Crates |
|---|---|
| Chat runtime, messages, branches, tools, no UI | `ai-ui-core` (always) |
| Talk to an AI SDK backend | `ai-ui-data-stream` + `ai-ui-http` |
| State and actions for any UI toolkit (`ThreadView`) | `ai-ui-state` |
| Markdown for streamed replies in your own renderer | `ai-ui-markdown` |
| Result-aware copy to the clipboard | `ai-ui-clipboard` |
| The ready-made Slint chat UI | `ai-ui-slint` (build-dependency) + `ai-ui-markdown-slint` + `ai-ui-state` |
| Custom wire protocol work, assistant-transport SSE | `ai-ui-stream` |
| Strict AI SDK 7 UI message stream reducer, standalone | `ai-ui-sdk-stream` |

Most apps need `ai-ui-core`, `ai-ui-state`, `ai-ui-data-stream` and `ai-ui-http`. Details per crate: [reference/crates.md](reference/crates.md).

## Hard rules

**Executor.** The runtime has no executor of its own. Runtime methods do their synchronous work at once and return a future (`RunFuture`) that you must spawn. Drive it with what the project already uses: `slint::spawn_local`, a Tokio `LocalSet`, or `wasm-bindgen-futures`. Use `futures_executor::block_on` only in tests and scripts. If the project has no executor and no UI, say so and ask which to use. See [reference/runtime.md](reference/runtime.md).

**Single thread.** Runtimes are `Rc`-based and single-threaded by design. Never wrap them in `Arc` or `Mutex`, and never move them to a multi-threaded executor. Messages are `Arc` snapshots, so adapters may move them to worker threads.

**Rust versions.** Minimum Rust 1.85 for the runtime crates. `ai-ui-clipboard` needs 1.86, `ai-ui-markdown` 1.88, `ai-ui-slint` and `ai-ui-markdown-slint` 1.92. Do not lower these. If the project's toolchain is older, tell the user.

**Slint.** Pin `slint` and `slint-build` to `=1.18.1`, with the feature `compat-1-18` on `slint`. `ai-ui-slint` is a build-dependency. In `build.rs`, register `ai_ui_slint::ui_dir()` as the library path named `assistant`, then import from `@assistant/lib.slint`. Full steps: [reference/slint-ui.md](reference/slint-ui.md).

**femtovg patch.** Until a Slint release uses femtovg 0.28, add this to the workspace root `Cargo.toml`. Without it a streaming chat uses about twice the CPU with Slint's FemtoVG-WGPU renderer. Slint's software and Skia renderers are not affected.

```toml
[patch.crates-io]
femtovg = { git = "https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust" }
```

**Linux.** Slint needs the fontconfig development package: `libfontconfig1-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu, `fontconfig-devel` on Fedora. The runtime and state crates do not need it.

**Licences.** The ai-ui crates are MIT, except `ai-ui-sdk-stream`, which is "MIT AND Apache-2.0". Slint is GPL-3.0, or royalty-free with an attribution badge, or commercial. Ask the user which Slint licence applies before shipping anything that uses the Slint crates. Do not choose for them. See [THIRD_PARTY.md](https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/blob/main/THIRD_PARTY.md).

**AI SDK backend.** The client posts model messages. The server passes `body.messages` straight to `streamText` (no `convertToModelMessages`) and returns `result.toUIMessageStreamResponse()`. The system prompt is a top-level `system` field, not a system-role message, because AI SDK 7 rejects system-role messages inside `messages` by default. Proxies must not buffer the response. See [reference/backend.md](reference/backend.md).

**Cumulative results.** A `ChatModelAdapter` yields the whole reply so far in each item, not a delta. A hand-written adapter must mark streaming text parts `PartStatus::Running` or the view will not pace them. The wire decoders do this for you.

**wasm32.** Use `FetchClient` instead of `NativeClient`; pick with `cfg(target_arch = "wasm32")`. The Slint crates reach the browser only through an app built like `examples/thread`. See [reference/web.md](reference/web.md).

## Verification checklist

Run each, in the user's project:
1. `cargo build` (and `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` for the crates that should build there, if the project targets the web).
2. `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`
3. `cargo test`
4. Run the app or a small example that sends one message and shows the streamed reply. Without a live backend, use a canned `ChatModelAdapter` or the loopback client in [reference/backend.md](reference/backend.md).

Report three lists: what you changed, what you ran (with results), and what you could not verify (for example a live backend, a GPU window, a licence decision).

## Known limits

Say these up front when they matter to the user's plan.
- Version 0.1, early. The repository does not call it production ready.
- Not yet ported: assistant-transport as a runtime (the wire format is decoded), a concrete HTTP remote thread-list adapter, LangGraph and other framework adapters.
- Not yet ported: custom per-tool components (generative UI). Tools render through a generic disclosure; an app can set a presenter per tool with `ThreadView::set_tool_presenter`.
- Not yet ported: attachment, feedback, speech, dictation, suggestion and history adapters, the message queue, composer attachments and quotes.
- Tools run sequentially.
- The Slint crates need the femtovg patch above. Markdown styling fidelity in a real GPU window is marked unverified in [STATUS](https://github.com/iyiolacak/ai-ui-rewrite-rust/blob/main/docs/STATUS.md).
- The interop test covers an AI SDK 7 `streamText` server only. Other backends, authentication and retries are not covered.
- In the browser build of the example, there are no Markdown worker threads and the example runs only its demo model; use `FetchClient` in your own app.
- Performance figures in the README are measured on one machine. Do not quote them as guarantees. See the README and `docs/RESULTS.md`.
